modules.title: C: programming without a safety net
modules.summary: Write, build and debug real C: the compile/link pipeline, fixed-size types, pointers, strings, structs and manual memory, checked with gdb/lldb and ASan.

lessons.title: From source file to running program
lessons.objective: By the end you can run each stage of the C build pipeline by hand and say which stage produced a given error.
concept: Python hides the build; C makes you own it. `cc hello.c -o hello` actually runs four programs. The **preprocessor** handles lines starting with `#`: it pastes the text of `#include` files and does textual `#define` substitution. The **compiler** turns that expanded C into assembly for your CPU. The **assembler** turns assembly into an **object file** (`hello.o`): real machine code, but with holes where it calls functions defined elsewhere, like `printf`.

The **linker** stitches object files and libraries together and fills those holes by matching **symbols** (names of functions and globals). If `main.o` calls `add` and no object file defines `add`, the compiler is happy but the linker fails with `undefined reference to 'add'` (Linux) or `Undefined symbols ... _add` (macOS). Headers (`.h`) hold **declarations** ("this exists"); `.c` files hold **definitions** ("here it is"). Define a global in a header included twice and you get `multiple definition`.

You can stop after any stage: `cc -E` (preprocess only), `cc -S` (emit assembly), `cc -c` (emit `.o`). Libraries come in two kinds: **static** (`.a`, copied into your executable) and **shared** (`.so` / `.dylib`, loaded at run time by the dynamic loader). When you finally run `./hello`, the OS **loader** maps the executable into memory, loads shared libraries such as libc, and jumps to its entry point, which eventually calls `main`.

example.code:
# mymath.h declares: int add(int a, int b);
# mymath.c defines add; main.c calls it
cc -c mymath.c        # -> mymath.o (defines symbol add)
cc -c main.c          # -> main.o (references add, unresolved)
cc main.o mymath.o -o app   # linker resolves add
nm main.o | grep add  # 'U _add' (macOS) / 'U add' (Linux): undefined here
nm mymath.o | grep add  # 'T _add': defined in the text section
./app
example.explain: Compiling each file separately with `-c` is how real projects build: change one file, recompile one `.o`, relink. `nm` lists symbols: `U` means used-but-undefined, `T` means defined in the code (text) section. Leave `mymath.o` off the link line and you get the classic undefined-symbol error.

lessons.tryit: Create `main.c`, `mymath.c` and `mymath.h` as in the example. Run `cc -E main.c | tail -20` and find your declaration pasted in. Run `cc -S mymath.c` and open `mymath.s`. Then deliberately link without `mymath.o`, copy the exact error, and write one sentence explaining which stage produced it and why.

questions.prompt: Which stage turns the call to `printf` in your object file into a call to the actual code in libc?
options: The compiler, when it generates assembly
The linker (and dynamic loader for shared libc)
The assembler, when it encodes the call instruction
questions.explain: `#include <stdio.h>` only pastes a declaration of `printf`, which tells the compiler its signature. The object file still has an unresolved reference; the linker records it and the dynamic loader binds it to libc's code at load time. The preprocessor never sees function bodies.

questions.prompt: What does this print? (Remember the preprocessor does text substitution.)
questions.explain: The macro expands textually to `1 + 2 * 1 + 2`, and `*` binds tighter than `+`, giving 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, not 9. The fix is to parenthesize: `#define SQ(x) ((x) * (x))`. This is why the preprocessor is a separate, dumb stage: it knows nothing about C expressions.

questions.prompt: `cc main.c -o app` fails with `Undefined symbols for architecture arm64: "_parse_config"`. `main.c` includes `config.h`, which declares `parse_config`. What is wrong?
options: `config.h` has a syntax error the compiler could not report
`config.c`, which defines `parse_config`, was not compiled and linked in
`parse_config` must be declared `static` to be visible
You need `#include "config.c"` instead of the header
questions.explain: The message comes from the linker: compilation succeeded because the declaration in `config.h` satisfied the compiler. Nothing on the link line defines the symbol, so run `cc main.c config.c -o app`. Making it `static` would hide it from other files, and including a `.c` file works by accident but breaks as soon as two files do it (multiple definitions).

questions.prompt: Arrange the commands to build `hello` one stage at a time, then run it.
questions.explain: Each command consumes the previous command's output file: `.c` to `.i` (preprocessed) to `.s` (assembly) to `.o` (object) to the linked executable, which can only run after it exists.

video.title: How does GCC compile C code to an executable

lessons.why: When a C or C++ build fails, knowing which stage produced the error tells you where to look. The same pipeline sits under Rust, Go and every native library Python uses.

terms.d: Handles `#include` and `#define` by pasting and replacing text.
Turns one preprocessed file into assembly, then an object file.
Machine code for one source file, with holes for symbols defined elsewhere.
Joins object files and libraries by matching symbol names.

mistakes.wrong: An 'undefined reference' error means my code has a syntax error.
mistakes.right: It's a linker error: something is declared but no object file or library defines it. Check what you're linking.

mistakes.wrong: A header file contains the function's code.
mistakes.right: Headers usually hold declarations. The definitions live in a `.c` file or library that must be linked.

takeaways: `cc` runs preprocessor, compiler, assembler and linker in sequence.
Use `-E`, `-S` and `-c` to stop after each stage and inspect the output.
Static libraries are copied in at link time; shared ones are loaded at run time.

lessons.title: Types, sizes and integer traps
lessons.objective: By the end you can state the size of common C types on a 64-bit system and predict the result of unsigned wraparound, integer division and mixed signed/unsigned comparisons.
concept: In Python an `int` grows forever. In C every type is a fixed number of bytes and the bits simply run out. The standard only fixes `sizeof(char) == 1`; everything else is a minimum. On 64-bit Linux and macOS (the **LP64** model) `short` is 2 bytes, `int` 4, `long` 8, `long long` 8 and every pointer 8. On 64-bit Windows `long` is only 4. When the size matters, use `<stdint.h>`: `int32_t`, `uint8_t`, `uint64_t`. `sizeof` yields a `size_t`; print it with `%zu`.

**Unsigned** arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^n: a `uint8_t` holding 255 plus 1 is 0. **Signed** overflow is **undefined behavior**: `INT_MAX + 1` may wrap, crash, or let the optimizer delete your overflow check, because the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens. Integer division truncates toward zero, so `-7 / 2` is `-3` and `-7 % 2` is `-1` (Python gives -4 and 1, because it floors).

C silently converts types in expressions. Anything narrower than `int` is **promoted** to `int` first. When a signed and an unsigned value of the same rank meet, the signed one is converted to unsigned. So `-1 < 1u` is false: -1 becomes 4294967295. The same trap appears as `for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)`, which never ends because a `size_t` is never negative. Compile with `-Wall -Wextra` and the compiler warns about most of these.

example.explain: On a 64-bit Mac or Linux box this prints `int=4 long=8 ptr=8`, then `b=0`, then `-3 -1`. `b + 1` is computed as an `int` (256) and converting it back to `uint8_t` keeps it modulo 256.

lessons.tryit: Write `sizes.c` that prints `sizeof` for `char`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `long long`, `float`, `double`, `void *` and `size_t`. Then add a loop `for (unsigned i = 3; i >= 0; i--)` that prints `i`, predict what happens before you run it, compile with `-Wall -Wextra`, and read the warning.

questions.prompt: Which statement does the C standard guarantee on every platform?
questions.explain: Only `sizeof(char) == 1` is guaranteed (sizes are measured in chars). `int` is 4 on all mainstream desktop platforms but 2 on some microcontrollers, and `long` is 4 on 64-bit Windows, which also breaks the pointer-equals-long assumption.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `c + 10` is computed as `int` 260, then stored back into an 8-bit unsigned char, which keeps the value modulo 256: 260 - 256 = 4. Unsigned wraparound is fully defined, unlike signed overflow.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: C division truncates toward zero, so -3.5 becomes -3, and the remainder satisfies (a/b)*b + a%b == a, giving -1. Python's `//` floors instead, so `-7 // 2` is -4 and `-7 % 2` is 1. Porting Python code to C without noticing this is a classic bug.

questions.prompt: This prints `no`. Why?
options: `1u` is a float literal, so the comparison is inexact
-1 is converted to unsigned (4294967295 with 32-bit int), which is not less than 1
Comparing signed and unsigned values is undefined behavior, so anything can happen
questions.explain: With `int` and `unsigned int` in one comparison, the usual arithmetic conversions turn the signed operand into unsigned. -1 becomes UINT_MAX, so the test is false. This is well-defined (not UB), which is exactly why it is dangerous: no crash, just a wrong branch. `-Wall -Wextra` warns about signed/unsigned comparison.

video.title: Understanding Signed vs Unsigned Integers in C

lessons.why: Fixed-size integers cause real security bugs and wrong answers. Predicting wraparound, promotion and signed/unsigned comparisons is basic C literacy.

terms.d: The 64-bit Unix model: `int` is 4 bytes, `long` and pointers are 8.
Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^n, by definition.
Code the standard gives no meaning to, like signed overflow; anything can happen.
Types narrower than `int` become `int` before arithmetic.

mistakes.wrong: `INT_MAX + 1` safely wraps to `INT_MIN`.
mistakes.right: Signed overflow is undefined behavior; the optimizer may assume it never happens and delete your check.

mistakes.wrong: `-1 < 1u` is true.
mistakes.right: The signed `-1` is converted to unsigned (a huge number), so the comparison is false.

takeaways: Only `sizeof(char) == 1` is fixed; use `<stdint.h>` types when size matters.
Unsigned wraps; signed overflow is undefined.
Mixed signed/unsigned comparisons convert to unsigned; compiler warnings catch them.

lessons.title: Pointers and arrays
lessons.objective: By the end you can draw memory diagrams for pointer code, use pointers to modify a caller's variables, and predict the result of pointer arithmetic over an array.
concept: A **pointer** is a variable whose value is a memory address. `&x` gives the address of `x`; `*p` follows the address to the value there. If `int x = 42; int *p = &x;`, then `*p = 7;` changes `x`. The pointer's type matters: it tells the compiler how many bytes to read at that address and how to interpret them. A pointer that points nowhere should be `NULL`; dereferencing `NULL` or a pointer to freed or out-of-scope memory is undefined behavior and usually a segfault.

C passes every argument **by value**: the function gets a copy. That is why `void inc(int n) { n++; }` changes nothing for the caller. To let a function modify your variable, pass its address: `void inc(int *n) { (*n)++; }` called as `inc(&x)`. This is also how C "returns" several values (`scanf`, `swap`) and why big structs are passed as `const struct big *` instead of being copied.

Arrays are contiguous blocks of elements. In most expressions an array name **decays** to a pointer to its first element, so `int *p = a;` works and `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`. Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the element size: if `p` is an `int *` at address 0x1000, `p + 1` is 0x1004. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives a count of elements, not bytes. Decay is also why a function parameter `int arr[]` is really `int *arr`: inside the function, `sizeof arr` is the size of a pointer and the length is lost. Always pass the length separately.

items.detail: 4 bytes holding 42

items.label: p  @ 0x7ffc0018

items.label: *p
items.detail: follow p to 0x7ffc0010 and read an int: 42

example.explain: `swap` receives copies of two addresses and writes through them, so the caller's variables change. The loop walks a pointer from the first element to one-past-the-end, which is the idiom behind every C string and buffer routine.

lessons.tryit: On paper, draw boxes for `x`, `y`, `a` and `b` (with made-up addresses) at the moment `swap` executes `*a = *b;`. Then write `void min_max(const int *arr, size_t n, int *min, int *max)` that reports both values through pointers, and call it from `main` on a 6-element array.

questions.prompt: After `int x = 5; int *p = &x;`, what is the value of `*p`?
options: 5, the value stored at the address `p` holds
questions.explain: `p` holds the address of `x`; the unary `*` dereferences that address and yields the int stored there, 5. `&p` would be the address of the pointer itself.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `f` gets a copy of `x` and changes only its copy, so `x` is still 1. `g` gets a copy of the address of `x` and writes through it, so `x` becomes 20. Passing the pointer is the only way a C function can change a caller's local variable.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `p += 2` moves two elements (8 bytes with 4-byte ints), landing on `a[2]` = 30. Subtracting pointers into the same array counts elements, not bytes, so `p - a` is 2. `%td` is the format for `ptrdiff_t`, the type of a pointer difference.

questions.prompt: On a typical 64-bit system, `count` prints 2 for a 10-element array. Why?
options: `sizeof` does not work on arrays of `int`
Inside `count`, `arr` is an `int *`, so `sizeof arr` is 8 (pointer) and 8 / 4 = 2
The array was copied and truncated when passed
questions.explain: An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer, so the size information is gone; `sizeof arr` gives the pointer size (8 on LP64) divided by `sizeof(int)` (4). The array was not copied at all, only its address. Clang even warns: 'sizeof on array function parameter will return size of int *'. Pass `n` explicitly.

lessons.why: Pointers are how C passes data around, builds data structures and talks to hardware. Drawing memory diagrams is the reliable way to reason about them.

Address-of and dereference: `p = &x` then `*p = 7` changes `x`.

An array name becomes a pointer to its first element in most expressions.

mistakes.wrong: `void inc(int n) { n++; }` increments the caller's variable.
mistakes.right: It increments a copy. Take `int *n` and write `(*n)++`.

mistakes.wrong: `p + 1` moves one byte forward.
mistakes.right: Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the pointed-to type: one `int` is 4 bytes.

`a[i]` means `*(a + i)`.
To change something in a function, pass its address.

lessons.title: Strings, structs and the heap
lessons.objective: By the end you can lay out a struct in memory, allocate and free heap objects correctly, and spot the off-by-one in C string code.
concept: A C **string** is just a `char` array ending in a zero byte, `'\0'`. There is no length field: `strlen` walks until it finds the zero, which is O(n). So `"cat"` needs 4 bytes, and every buffer you allocate for a string needs `strlen(s) + 1`. String literals live in read-only memory; writing to `char *s = "cat"; s[0] = 'b';` is undefined behavior, while `char s[] = "cat";` makes a writable copy. `strcpy` and `strcat` do no bounds checking; prefer `snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, ...)`.

A **struct** groups fields into one block. The compiler inserts **padding** so each field sits at an address that is a multiple of its alignment: on typical 64-bit systems `struct { char c; int i; }` is 8 bytes, not 5. Reach a field through a pointer with `p->field`, which means `(*p).field`. Assigning one struct to another copies every byte, unlike Python, where assignment copies a reference.

Local variables die when their function returns. For data that must outlive the call, ask the **heap**: `malloc(n)` returns a pointer to n uninitialised bytes or `NULL`; `calloc(count, size)` returns zeroed memory; `free(p)` gives it back. Every successful allocation must be freed exactly once. The classic bugs are **leaks** (never freed), **double free**, **use-after-free** (reading a pointer after `free`) and **buffer overflows** (writing past the end). Setting a pointer to `NULL` after freeing it turns a silent use-after-free into a clean crash.

lessons.tryit: Write `struct person { char name[32]; int age; };` and a function `struct person *person_new(const char *name, int age)` that heap-allocates one, copies the name safely with `snprintf`, and returns it. Print `sizeof(struct person)` and explain the number. Free everything and confirm with ASan (next lesson) that nothing leaks.

questions.prompt: What does `malloc(64)` give you when it succeeds?
options: A pointer to 64 bytes of uninitialised heap memory
A pointer to 64 bytes that are freed automatically when the function returns
64 bytes of zeroed heap memory, like `calloc`
questions.explain: `malloc` returns uninitialised heap memory that stays allocated until you call `free`. Only `calloc` guarantees zeros. Stack memory is what local variables use, and it is the stack, not the heap, that is released on return.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `printf("%s")` and `strlen` both stop at the first zero byte, now at index 3, so they see `abc` and 3. `sizeof s` is the array's size, fixed at compile time: 6 letters plus the original terminator = 7. Writing a zero shortens the string, never the array.

questions.prompt: On a typical x86-64 or ARM64 system, what is `sizeof(struct s)` for `struct s { char a; int b; char c; };`?
questions.explain: `a` at offset 0, 3 bytes padding so `b` is 4-aligned (offset 4), `c` at offset 8, then 3 bytes of tail padding so the struct size is a multiple of 4 (needed in arrays of structs): 12. Reordering to `int b; char a; char c;` gives 8. Padding is implementation-defined, which is why the question says 'typical'.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in this function?
options: It allocates `strlen(s)` bytes but copies `strlen(s) + 1` (the terminator), overflowing the block by one byte
`malloc` must be cast to `char *` in C
questions.explain: `strcpy` always writes the trailing `'\0'`, so it needs one byte more than `strlen` reports. The overflow corrupts the heap silently and may only crash much later, which is why you run tests under ASan. Casting `malloc`'s result is unnecessary in C.

video.title: How to manage memory with malloc, calloc, realloc, and free in C

lessons.why: Strings, structs and heap memory are where most C bugs and security holes live. Knowing their layout and lifetimes prevents overflows, leaks and use-after-free.

terms.d: A `char` array ending in `'\0'`; there's no stored length.
Bytes the compiler adds so each struct field is aligned.
Request heap memory and give it back; you own its lifetime.
Reading or writing memory after it has been freed.

mistakes.wrong: `"cat"` needs 3 bytes.
mistakes.right: It needs 4: three characters plus the terminating `'\0'`.

mistakes.wrong: `sizeof(struct { char c; int i; })` is 5.
mistakes.right: Padding aligns the `int`, so it's typically 8.

takeaways: Every buffer needs room for the terminating zero.
Struct size includes padding; order fields to reduce it.
Every `malloc` needs exactly one `free`, and nothing may use the pointer afterwards.

lessons.title: Debugging crashes: gdb/lldb, ASan, Valgrind
lessons.objective: By the end you can take a segfaulting program, get a backtrace in gdb or lldb, inspect variables in the crashing frame, and catch silent memory errors with AddressSanitizer.
concept: A **segmentation fault** (SIGSEGV, or `EXC_BAD_ACCESS` on macOS) means your process touched an address it has no right to: `NULL`, freed memory that was returned to the OS, past the end of the stack, or a garbage pointer. Step one is always to rebuild with debug info and no optimisation: `cc -g -O0`. Step two is to run it under a debugger instead of guessing with `printf`.

In **gdb** (Linux) or **lldb** (macOS): `run` starts the program and stops at the crash. `bt` prints the **backtrace**: frame #0 is where it died, higher frames are its callers. `frame 2` (gdb) or `frame select 2` (lldb) moves to a caller; `print expr` (or `p`) shows a value; `info locals` / `frame variable` shows all locals. `break file.c:12`, `next`, `step` and `continue` let you walk up to the bug before it happens. The crash site is often innocent: `strlen` crashing usually means someone passed it a bad pointer.

Many memory bugs never crash, they just corrupt data. **AddressSanitizer** (`cc -g -fsanitize=address`) instruments every load and store and stops at the first heap-buffer-overflow, stack-buffer-overflow, use-after-free or double free, printing where the bad access happened and where the memory was allocated and freed. It costs about 2x in speed, so use it for all tests. Leaks are reported at exit on Linux. **Valgrind** (`valgrind --leak-check=full ./prog`) needs no recompile but runs 20-50x slower and does not support Apple Silicon Macs; there, use ASan and the `leaks` tool.

example.code:
$ cc -g -O0 -o crash crash.c
$ lldb ./crash            # or: gdb ./crash
(lldb) run
* stop reason = EXC_BAD_ACCESS (code=1, address=0x0)
(lldb) bt                 # frame #0 strlen, #1 greet(name=0x0) at crash.c:6, #2 main at crash.c:12
(lldb) frame select 1
(lldb) p name             # (const char *) $0 = NULL
(lldb) quit
$ cc -g -fsanitize=address -o crash crash.c && ./crash
# ==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000 ... READ memory access
example.explain: The crash is in libc's `strlen`, but frame #1 shows `greet` received `name = NULL`, and frame #2 shows the line in `main` that passed it. The fix belongs in the code that produced the NULL, not in `strlen`. The gdb commands are the same apart from `frame 1` instead of `frame select 1`.

lessons.tryit: Write a 20-line program with one deliberate bug of each kind: an off-by-one heap write, a use-after-free and a leak (put each behind a command-line switch). Run each under ASan and, for each report, copy the first line of the error and the source line it points to. Then crash a NULL dereference under gdb or lldb and practise `bt`, `frame`, `p` and `info locals` / `frame variable`.

questions.prompt: Your program just crashed inside gdb. Which command shows the chain of function calls that led to the crash?
questions.explain: `bt` prints one line per stack frame, from the crashing function (#0) up to `main` and beyond. `list` shows source around the current line, `info registers` dumps CPU registers, and `next` steps a line, which is impossible after a fatal signal.

questions.prompt: Which build line enables AddressSanitizer with useful line numbers in its reports?
questions.explain: `-fsanitize=address` adds the instrumentation and links the ASan runtime; `-g` adds debug info so reports name files and lines. Warnings (`-Wall`) catch some bugs at compile time but cannot see run-time memory errors.

questions.prompt: A crash produces this backtrace. Where should you look first for the bug?
questions.code:
#0 strlen ()
#1 print_name (name=0x0) at main.c:8
#2 main () at main.c:15
#3 start ()
options: Inside `strlen`: libc has a bug with long strings
`main.c:15`, where `main` passes a NULL `name`, and wherever that NULL came from
Frame #3, `start`, because it is the first frame to run
questions.explain: Library functions like `strlen` are almost never the bug; they crash because they were given bad input. Walk up the stack to the first frame that is your code and has a suspicious value: `name=0x0` arrives from `main.c:15`. Then ask why that pointer was NULL (a failed lookup? an unchecked malloc?).

questions.prompt: ASan stops a test with `heap-use-after-free`. Which code pattern produces exactly that report?
questions.explain: Reading `*p` after `free(p)` touches freed heap memory: heap-use-after-free. Freeing twice is reported as `attempting double-free`, `a[4]` on a local array is a `stack-buffer-overflow`, and a missing free is a leak reported by LeakSanitizer at exit.

video.title: Find Memory Leaks and Buffer Overrun Using Valgrind and AddressSanitizer (ASAN)

lessons.why: Crashes and silent memory corruption are inevitable in C. A debugger and sanitizers turn a mysterious segfault into the exact line and variable in minutes.

terms.d: The process touched memory it has no right to.
The chain of calls at the crash; frame #0 is where it died.
`-fsanitize=address`: stops at the first out-of-bounds or use-after-free access.
Runs the program on a simulated CPU to find leaks and invalid accesses.

mistakes.wrong: If the program doesn't crash, it has no memory bugs.
mistakes.right: Many overflows silently corrupt data. Run with AddressSanitizer to find them.

mistakes.wrong: The crash line in frame #0 is always where the bug is.
mistakes.right: That's where the bad access happened; the bad pointer often came from a caller. Walk up the frames.

takeaways: Compile with `-g` and run in gdb or lldb; `bt` shows the backtrace.
Inspect variables in the crashing frame, then move up to callers.
Use ASan during development to catch silent memory errors.

project.title: A string library and linked list in C, clean under ASan
project.brief: Implement `mystr.c` (your own `my_strlen`, `my_strcpy`, `my_strdup`, `my_strcmp`, `my_strsplit`) and `list.c` (a singly linked list of heap-allocated strings) with headers and a test program. It forces you to manage every byte yourself and prove, with AddressSanitizer, that you never overflow, leak or touch freed memory.

lessons.title: Binary, hex and two's complement
lessons.objective: By the end you can convert between binary, hex and decimal, and encode or decode negative numbers in n-bit two's complement by hand.
concept: Every value in a computer is a row of bits. Binary is base 2: `1011` is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. **Hex** is base 16 and exists because one hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits: `0xFF` = `1111 1111` = 255, and `0x2A` = `0010 1010` = 42. Learn the nibbles 0-F by heart; reading memory dumps, addresses and colour codes becomes instant. Python helps you check: `bin(42)`, `hex(42)`, `int('2a', 16)`.

**Two's complement** is how CPUs store signed integers. In n bits the top bit has weight -2^(n-1) instead of +2^(n-1). For 8 bits: `1000 0000` is -128 and `1111 1111` is -128 + 127 = -1. To negate, invert all bits and add 1: 5 = `0000 0101`, invert `1111 1010`, add 1 = `1111 1011` = -5. The range is asymmetric, -128..127, so -(-128) does not fit in 8 bits.

The beauty is that the same adder circuit works for signed and unsigned numbers: `1111 1111 + 0000 0001` gives `0000 0000` either way (255 + 1 wraps to 0, or -1 + 1 = 0). Only interpretation differs, which is why C has signed and unsigned types over the same bits. **Sign extension** copies the top bit when widening (`int8_t` -1 becomes `int32_t` -1 = `0xFFFFFFFF`). Finally, **endianness**: x86-64 and ARM64 are little-endian, storing the least significant byte at the lowest address.

example.code:
x = -5
bits = x & 0xFF                 # the 8-bit two's complement pattern
print(format(bits, '08b'), hex(bits))   # 11111011 0xfb
print(bits - 256 if bits & 0x80 else bits)  # decode back: -5
print(int('11111011', 2), 0xFB)         # 251 251 as unsigned
example.explain: Python integers are unbounded, so masking with `0xFF` is how you see the low 8 bits a CPU register would hold. Decoding checks the sign bit (0x80) and subtracts 2^8 if it is set.

lessons.tryit: Without a computer, convert 0xC8, 0x3F and 0x80 to binary and to unsigned and signed 8-bit decimal. Then encode -1, -37 and -128 as 8-bit two's complement. Check every answer with the Python example and write down any you got wrong and why.

questions.prompt: What is 0x2A in decimal?
questions.explain: 0x2A = 2 * 16 + 10 = 42. Reading it as decimal 2-and-A or treating A as 1 gives the wrong answers; each hex digit is 4 bits (`0010 1010`).

questions.prompt: What does this Python print?
questions.code: print((-6) & 0xFF)
questions.explain: Masking with 0xFF keeps the low 8 bits of -6 in two's complement: 256 - 6 = 250 (`1111 1010`). Python's `&` on a negative int behaves as if the number had infinitely many leading 1 bits, so you get the same pattern a CPU would.

questions.prompt: What is -20 in 8-bit two's complement?
questions.explain: 20 = `0001 0100`; inverting gives `1110 1011` (that is ones' complement, the tempting wrong answer); adding 1 gives `1110 1100`. Check: 236 - 256 = -20. `1001 0100` is sign-magnitude, which CPUs do not use for integers.

questions.prompt: A `uint32_t` holding 0x11223344 is stored at address 0x100 on a little-endian machine (x86-64 or ARM64). Which byte is at address 0x100?
questions.explain: Little-endian stores the least significant byte first, so memory from 0x100 upward reads 44 33 22 11. A debugger's byte view shows this reversed order, while its word view shows 0x11223344. Network protocols use big-endian, which is why `htonl` exists.

lessons.title: Bitwise operators and masks
lessons.objective: By the end you can set, clear, toggle and test individual bits, and read idioms like `x & (x - 1)` in real code.
concept: Bitwise operators work on every bit position independently: `&` (AND: 1 only if both are 1), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR: 1 if they differ), `~` (NOT: flip every bit), and shifts `<<` and `>>`. `x << k` multiplies by 2^k, `x >> k` divides an unsigned value by 2^k. In C, right-shifting a negative signed value is implementation-defined, and shifting by the type's width or more is undefined, so do bit work on unsigned types.

A **mask** selects bits. With `1u << k` as the bit you care about: set it with `x | (1u << k)`, clear it with `x & ~(1u << k)`, toggle it with `x ^ (1u << k)`, and test it with `(x >> k) & 1`. To pull out a field, shift then mask: the high nibble of a byte is `(b >> 4) & 0xF`. Unix permissions are a bitmask (`0755` octal), as are flags like `O_CREAT | O_TRUNC` passed to `open`.

Two idioms show up everywhere. `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so for `x > 0`, `(x & (x - 1)) == 0` tests for a power of two, and counting how many times you can do it before reaching 0 counts the set bits (**popcount**). `x & -x` isolates the lowest set bit (it is the core of Fenwick trees). Watch C precedence: `&`, `^` and `|` bind more loosely than `==`, so `x & 1 == 0` means `x & (1 == 0)`. Always parenthesize.

example.explain: `popcount` runs once per set bit, not once per bit position, because `x &= x - 1` removes one set bit per iteration. Real code calls `__builtin_popcount`, which compiles to a single instruction on modern CPUs.

questions.prompt: Which expression clears bit 3 of `unsigned x` and leaves all other bits unchanged?
questions.explain: `~(1u << 3)` is all ones except bit 3, so ANDing keeps every other bit and forces bit 3 to 0. `|` sets the bit, `^` toggles it (which sets it if it was clear), and `& (1u << 3)` clears every other bit instead.

questions.prompt: What does this Python print?
questions.explain: `~x` is `-x - 1` for Python's unbounded two's-complement ints, so `~5` is -6, not 2 or 250. `5 ^ 3` is `101 ^ 011` = `110` = 6 (XOR, not exponentiation; Python uses `**` for powers). `1 << 10` is 2^10 = 1024.

questions.prompt: For an unsigned `n`, what does `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` tell you?
options: n is a power of two, or n is 0
n has exactly two set bits
questions.explain: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and every bit below it, so the AND clears exactly that lowest set bit. The result is 0 only if there was at most one set bit: a power of two, or 0 itself (where 0 - 1 wraps to all ones and 0 & anything is 0). Real code writes `n && !(n & (n - 1))` to exclude 0.

lessons.title: Floating point: why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain the IEEE 754 double layout, predict when float arithmetic is inexact, and compare and accumulate floats safely.
concept: A 64-bit **double** is scientific notation in base 2: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits, meaning value = (-1)^sign * 1.fraction * 2^(exponent - 1023). That gives about 15-17 significant decimal digits and a range up to about 1.8e308. A 32-bit **float** has 23 fraction bits, about 7 digits. Integers are exact up to 2^53 in a double; beyond that, only every second integer is representable, then every fourth, and so on.

0.1 in binary is `0.000110011001100...`, repeating forever, just like 1/3 in decimal. It must be rounded to 52 bits, so the stored value is 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.... The same happens to 0.2 and 0.3, and the rounding errors do not cancel: `0.1 + 0.2` produces the double just above the one nearest 0.3, printed as `0.30000000000000004`. This is not a Python bug; C, JavaScript and your GPU do exactly the same thing.

Practical rules. Never compare floats with `==` after arithmetic; use a tolerance: `math.isclose(a, b)` or `fabs(a - b) < 1e-9 * fabs(b)`. Floating-point addition is not associative: adding many small numbers to a big one loses them, so sum small-to-large or use `math.fsum`. Store money as integer cents or `Decimal`. Know the special values: `inf`, `-inf`, `-0.0`, and `nan`, which is not equal to anything, including itself, so `x != x` is the classic NaN test.

items.label: Sign: 1 bit
items.detail: 0 = positive, 1 = negative

items.label: Exponent: 11 bits
items.detail: stored with bias 1023; all ones = inf/NaN

items.label: Fraction: 52 bits
items.detail: digits after the implicit leading 1.

items.label: 0.1 as stored
items.detail: 0x3FB999999999999A: 1.6 * 2^-4, with the last bits rounded up

example.code:
import math, struct
from decimal import Decimal

print(0.1 + 0.2)                 # 0.30000000000000004
print(Decimal(0.1))              # the exact value actually stored
print(struct.pack('>d', 0.1).hex())   # 3fb999999999999a
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # True
total = 0.0
for _ in range(10):
    total += 0.1
print(total, math.fsum([0.1] * 10))  # 0.9999999999999999 1.0
example.explain: `Decimal(0.1)` reveals the exact binary value behind the literal. `struct.pack` shows the 64 raw bits: `3fb` is the sign and exponent, and the repeating `999...a` is the rounded fraction. The loop rounds after every `+=`; `math.fsum` tracks the lost low-order bits and returns the correctly rounded sum. (Since Python 3.12 the built-in `sum()` also compensates for float rounding, but C and most other languages do not.)

lessons.tryit: Predict, then run: `0.1 * 3 == 0.3`, `1e16 + 1 == 1e16`, `float('nan') == float('nan')`, `0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75`. For each, explain in one sentence why. Then write a function that sums a list of prices given as strings like "19.99" exactly, using integer cents.

questions.prompt: How many bits of a 64-bit IEEE 754 double store the fraction (mantissa)?
questions.explain: 1 sign + 11 exponent + 52 fraction = 64. The precision is effectively 53 bits because normal numbers have an implicit leading 1 that is not stored; 23 is the fraction width of a 32-bit float.

questions.prompt: What does this Python print?
questions.explain: `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004, a different double from the literal `0.3`, so `==` is False. Rounding to 10 decimal places lands on the same double as `0.3`, so the second test is True. Better practice than rounding is `math.isclose`.

questions.prompt: What does this Python print?
questions.code: print(float(2**53) == float(2**53 + 1))
questions.explain: A double has 53 bits of precision, so above 2^53 consecutive integers are no longer all representable. 2^53 + 1 rounds to 2^53 (round-half-to-even), so both sides are the same double. This is why JavaScript's `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is 2^53 - 1.

questions.prompt: `(1e16 + 1.0) - 1e16` evaluates to `0.0` in Python and C. Why?
options: Python truncates floats to 15 digits when adding
Near 1e16, adjacent doubles are 2 apart, so 1e16 + 1 rounds back to 1e16 before the subtraction
Subtraction of equal-looking numbers always returns 0.0
1.0 is converted to an integer first
questions.explain: Between 2^53 (about 9.0e15) and 2^54 the gap between representable doubles is 2. The exact sum 1e16 + 1 is a tie between 1e16 and 1e16 + 2 and rounds to the even one, 1e16, so the 1.0 is lost entirely. The subtraction itself is exact; the information vanished in the addition. Summing small values first avoids this.

lessons.title: From NAND to ALU
lessons.objective: By the end you can build NOT, AND, OR, XOR and a multiplexer from NAND gates, build an adder from them, and explain what the Hack ALU's control bits do.
concept: A logic gate is a tiny circuit that computes a Boolean function. **NAND** (`not (a and b)`) is **universal**: every other gate can be built from it. `NOT(a) = NAND(a, a)`; `AND(a, b) = NOT(NAND(a, b))`; `OR(a, b) = NAND(NOT a, NOT b)` by De Morgan's law. Nand2Tetris starts you with only NAND and has you build every chip of a computer, which is the clearest way to see that there is no magic between transistors and programs.

Arithmetic is just gates. A **half adder** adds two bits: `sum = XOR(a, b)`, `carry = AND(a, b)`. A **full adder** adds three bits (a, b, carry-in) using two half adders and an OR. Chain 16 full adders, each passing its carry to the next, and you have a 16-bit **ripple-carry adder**. Two's complement means the same adder subtracts: `x - y = x + NOT(y) + 1`. A **multiplexer** (`Mux`) picks one of two inputs with a select bit: `out = (a AND NOT sel) OR (b AND sel)`.

The Hack **ALU** takes two 16-bit inputs `x`, `y` and six control bits applied in order: `zx` (zero x), `nx` (negate, meaning bitwise NOT, x), `zy`, `ny`, `f` (1 = `x + y`, 0 = `x & y`) and `no` (NOT the output). Different bit patterns compute 18 functions, including `x + y`, `x - y`, `x & y`, `x | y`, `-x`, `x + 1`, 0, 1 and -1. Status outputs `zr` (output is zero) and `ng` (output is negative) are what jump instructions test. Everything above this, memory and the CPU, adds state with a clock.

lessons.title: How a CPU runs your code, and reading its assembly
lessons.objective: By the end you can describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle and read simple x86-64 and ARM64 compiler output to say what C produced it.
concept: A CPU is a loop in hardware. The **program counter** (PC, `rip` on x86-64) holds the address of the next instruction. **Fetch** reads the instruction bytes at the PC; **decode** works out the operation and operands; **execute** runs it on the ALU or computes an address; memory instructions then **load** or **store**; results are **written back** to registers; and the PC advances to the next instruction, or to a branch target. Registers are the CPU's tiny, fastest storage: 16 general-purpose ones on x86-64, 31 on ARM64.

Real CPUs **pipeline** these stages, working on many instructions at once, and even execute them out of order. Branches are a problem because the CPU must guess which way they go before knowing; a **misprediction** throws away 15-20 cycles of work. That is why a loop over sorted data with an `if` can be several times faster than the same loop over random data.

Read compiler output with `cc -O2 -S file.c` or paste code into Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org). The **calling convention** tells you where things live. On x86-64 Linux and macOS, the first integer arguments are in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9` (`edi`, `esi` for 32-bit ints) and the return value goes in `rax`/`eax`. On ARM64, arguments are in `x0`-`x7` (`w0`-`w7` for 32-bit) and the result goes in `x0`/`w0`. Optimised code is often shorter than you expect: the compiler turns multiplications into shifts and loops into formulas.

questions.prompt: What does the program counter hold?
options: The number of instructions executed so far
The address of the next instruction to fetch
The result of the last ALU operation
questions.explain: The PC (instruction pointer, `rip` on x86-64) is an address, not a count. Normally it advances by the instruction's length; jumps, calls and returns overwrite it. The top of the stack is in the stack pointer (`rsp` / `sp`).

questions.prompt: clang -O2 on ARM64 produces this for a function `int f(int x)`. Which C function is it?

f:
    lsl  w0, w0, #3
    ret
questions.explain: `lsl w0, w0, #3` shifts the argument left by 3 bits, multiplying by 2^3 = 8, and leaves it in `w0`, the return register. `x << 8` would be `#8`, and a signed division by 8 needs extra instructions to round negative numbers toward zero.

questions.prompt: A non-branch ARM64 instruction finishes executing. What does the PC become?
options: PC + 4, since every ARM64 instruction is 4 bytes
The address on top of the stack
questions.explain: ARM64 uses fixed 4-byte instructions, so sequential execution adds 4. x86-64 instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long, so there the PC advances by the length of whatever was decoded. Only `ret` takes the next PC from the stack (x86) or the link register (ARM).

questions.prompt: You compile `int sum(int n) { int s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += i; return s; }` with clang -O2 and the output has no loop or branch back, just a few multiply, shift and add instructions. Why?
options: The compiler failed to compile the loop and returns garbage
The compiler recognised the loop as an arithmetic series and replaced it with the closed form n(n-1)/2
Loops are always moved into a library call at -O2
The CPU executes loops in microcode so they do not appear in assembly
questions.explain: LLVM's induction-variable analysis recognises sum-of-0..n-1 and emits the formula, an O(1) computation equivalent to the O(n) loop. The output still handles n <= 0 by returning 0. This is why you benchmark and read assembly instead of assuming the machine runs your source literally.

terms.d: Holds the address of the next instruction (`rip` on x86-64).
Read the instruction, work out what it means, do it, write back.
Overlapping stages of many instructions; branch mispredictions flush it.
Where arguments and return values live, such as `rdi`, `rsi` and `rax` on x86-64.

mistakes.wrong: The CPU runs one instruction completely before starting the next.
mistakes.right: Modern CPUs pipeline and run instructions out of order; mispredicted branches cost cycles.

mistakes.wrong: Compiler output is unreadable.

exam.prompt: Bitmasks are how you enumerate subsets (as in DSA subset/bitmask DP). What does this print?
exam.explain: `range(1 << 4)` walks all 16 subsets of a 4-element set; the set bits of `mask` say which elements are in. Masks with exactly two bits set are the 2-element subsets: C(4, 2) = 6 (0011, 0101, 0110, 1001, 1010, 1100).

exam.prompt: What does this C program print? (Mind operator precedence.)
exam.explain: `>>` binds tighter than `&`, so this is `(0xF0 >> 4) & 0x3` = `0xF & 0x3` = 3. Here the precedence happens to match intent, but with `==` it would not: `x & 1 == 0` parses as `x & (1 == 0)`. Parenthesize bit expressions.

exam.prompt: The byte `1111 1111` is read as an 8-bit unsigned and then as an 8-bit signed value. What are the two values?
exam.explain: Unsigned: 128+64+...+1 = 255. Signed two's complement: the top bit weighs -128, so -128 + 127 = -1. -127 would be ones' complement or sign-magnitude thinking.

exam.prompt: Adding 0.1 ten times in a loop (`total += 0.1`, in Python or C) gives a total for which `total == 1.0` is False. What is the most robust fix for code that adds up many measurements and checks the total?
options: Use `math.fsum` for the sum and `math.isclose` for the comparison
Convert each value to `int` before summing
Switch to 32-bit floats, which round more
exam.explain: Each `+=` rounds, and ten roundings leave 0.9999999999999999. `math.fsum` returns the correctly rounded sum of the inputs, and `isclose` compares with a relative tolerance instead of exact bits. Rounding to 2 places hides the error only for some magnitudes, `int` truncates the data, and 32-bit floats are less precise.

exam.prompt: Which gate expression implements Mux(a, b, sel), which outputs a when sel=0 and b when sel=1?
options: (a AND sel) OR (b AND NOT sel)
(a AND NOT sel) OR (b AND sel)
exam.explain: When sel=0, `NOT sel` is 1, so the first term passes a and the second term is 0; when sel=1 the roles swap and b passes. Option 1 has the select inverted (b when sel=0). `(a AND b) OR sel` outputs 1 whenever sel=1, and XOR mixes all three inputs instead of choosing one. Check any candidate with an 8-row truth table.

exam.prompt: clang -O2 on ARM64 emits this for `int f(int a, int b)`. What does f compute?
exam.code:
f:
    cmp  w0, w1
    csel w0, w0, w1, gt
    ret
options: the larger of a and b
the smaller of a and b
exam.explain: `cmp w0, w1` compares a with b and sets flags; `csel w0, w0, w1, gt` selects w0 (a) if the 'greater than' condition holds, else w1 (b), into the return register. That is `a > b ? a : b`, a branchless max. The 0/1 version would use `cset`.

exam.prompt: Which test is true only when the double `x` is NaN?
exam.explain: NaN compares unequal to everything, including itself, so `x != x` is true only for NaN (prefer `isnan(x)` for readability). `x == NAN` is always false. `x == x + 1` is also true for infinities and for huge values like 1e300, so it is not a NaN test.

exam.prompt: Connecting to C types (Module 1): why can `if (x + 1 > x)` with `int x` be compiled to `if (1)` while the same test with `unsigned x` cannot?
options: Unsigned comparisons are slower, so the optimizer skips them
Signed overflow is undefined behavior, so the compiler may assume x + 1 never wraps; unsigned addition is defined to wrap, so x = UINT_MAX makes the test false
The two's complement adder cannot add 1 to a signed number
`int` is wider than `unsigned`, so it never overflows
exam.explain: The hardware wraps both identically (same adder, same bits). The difference is the language rule: because signed overflow is UB, the optimizer reasons as if it never happens, which makes `x + 1 > x` always true. For unsigned, UINT_MAX + 1 == 0 is required behavior, so the check must stay. This is why overflow checks must be written before the operation, e.g. `x < INT_MAX`.

modules.title: The memory hierarchy
modules.summary: Know where every byte lives and what it costs to reach: stack and heap layout, caches and locality, virtual memory, the TLB, and how malloc works.

lessons.title: The address space: stack vs heap
lessons.objective: By the end you can draw a process's memory layout, say which region any variable lives in, and explain why deep recursion crashes.
concept: Every process gets the illusion of one big private array of bytes, its **address space**. From low to high addresses: **text** (machine code, read-only), **rodata** (string literals, constants), **data** (initialised globals and `static`s), **bss** (zero-initialised globals, which take no space in the file), the **heap** growing upward, a region for `mmap`ed files and shared libraries, and the **stack** growing downward from near the top. The kernel's memory sits above all of it, inaccessible from user mode.

The **stack** holds one **frame** per active function call: its return address, saved registers, arguments that did not fit in registers, and local variables. Calling a function just subtracts from the stack pointer; returning adds back, so stack allocation is nearly free and automatic, but a frame vanishes on return. The stack is small: 8 MiB by default for a Linux or macOS main thread (`ulimit -s`), 512 KiB for secondary threads on macOS. Recurse a million levels deep and you hit an unmapped **guard page**: segfault.

The **heap** is for data whose size or lifetime is not known at compile time. `malloc` manages it, asking the kernel for more with `brk`/`sbrk` or `mmap`. Allocation costs tens of nanoseconds, the memory lives until `free`, and fragmentation is your problem. Because of **ASLR** (address space layout randomization), the base of each region moves every run, so pointer values printed in two runs differ; the relative layout does not.

questions.prompt: In which region does `static int hits;` (a global with no initialiser) live?
questions.explain: Zero-initialised globals and statics go in bss, which the loader fills with zeros, so they cost no space in the executable. They live for the whole run, unlike stack variables, and no `malloc` is involved, so they are not on the heap.

questions.prompt: Inside a function, `char *p = malloc(10);` runs. Where are `p` and the 10 bytes?
options: `p` on the stack; the 10 bytes on the heap
`p` on the heap; the 10 bytes on the stack
Both on the stack until `free` is called
questions.explain: `p` is an ordinary local variable (8 bytes in the function's frame) whose value is an address in the heap. When the function returns, `p` disappears; the heap block does not, which is how leaks happen if nobody else kept the address.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: A `static` local is stored in data/bss, not in the stack frame, so it is initialised once and keeps its value between calls: 1, 2, then 3. Without `static`, `n` would be a fresh stack variable each call and every call would return 1.

questions.prompt: A C function recurses to depth 1,000,000 with about 100 bytes per frame and segfaults; the same algorithm in Python raised `RecursionError` at depth 1000. What is happening in C, and what is the standard fix?
options: C has a 1,000,000-call limit; raise it with a compiler flag
~100 MB of frames overflow the ~8 MiB stack into a guard page; rewrite it iteratively with an explicit stack on the heap
The heap ran out; call `free` inside the recursion
Each call leaks memory; add `static` to the locals
questions.explain: 1,000,000 * 100 B is about 100 MB, far past the default 8 MiB stack, so the next frame lands on an unmapped guard page and the kernel sends SIGSEGV. Python checks depth itself and raises an exception before that. Converting to a loop with your own heap-allocated stack (as in iterative DFS) removes the limit; raising `ulimit -s` only moves it.

lessons.title: Caches and locality
lessons.objective: By the end you can quote the rough latency of each level of the memory hierarchy and predict which of two loops over the same data is faster and why.
concept: A modern core can do several operations per nanosecond, but fetching from main memory (DRAM) takes about **100 ns**, hundreds of cycles. Caches bridge the gap: small, fast SRAM close to the core. **L1** (~32-64 KiB per core) answers in ~1 ns (about 4 cycles), **L2** (~1 MiB) in ~4 ns, **L3** (tens of MiB, shared) in ~10-40 ns. Memory moves between levels in **cache lines** of 64 bytes on x86-64 (128 bytes on Apple M-series), never single bytes.

Caches win because programs have **locality**. **Temporal**: data used now is likely used again soon (a loop counter, a hot table). **Spatial**: data near what you used is likely next (the next array element). Reading one `int` brings in its whole line, so the next 15 `int`s are free. Hardware **prefetchers** detect sequential or strided streams and fetch lines before you ask. Random access defeats both, and every miss costs up to the full DRAM latency.

Consequences you can measure. C stores 2-D arrays **row-major**: `a[i][j]` and `a[i][j+1]` are adjacent. Looping `for i, for j` streams through memory; swapping to `for j, for i` jumps a whole row each step and can be 5-10x slower for a large array, with identical big-O. Likewise an array beats a linked list for traversal even though both are O(n): list nodes scattered on the heap turn every `->next` into a potential cache miss. Misses are classified as **compulsory** (first touch), **capacity** (working set too big) and **conflict** (addresses competing for the same cache set).

visual.title: Latency numbers to memorise (order of magnitude, ~2024 hardware)

example.explain: Both loops do the same 16.7 million additions. The row loop uses every byte of each 64-byte line it fetches; the column loop uses 4 bytes of each line and moves 16 KiB between accesses, so it misses constantly. Compile with `-O1` and expect the column version to be several times slower; the exact ratio depends on your CPU.

lessons.tryit: Run the example at `-O1` and record both times. Then change N to 256 (256 KiB total, which fits in L2) and run again: explain why the gap shrinks. Finally, sum 10 million ints stored in an array and in a linked list built in random order, and report the ratio.

questions.prompt: What is the size of a cache line on typical x86-64 CPUs?
questions.explain: Caches transfer 64-byte lines on x86-64 (Apple's M-series uses 128 bytes). 8 bytes is a word, and 4 KiB is a page, the unit of virtual memory, not of caching.

questions.prompt: `int a[1000][1000];` in C. Which loop nest makes better use of the cache when summing every element?
options: Both are identical because both are O(n^2)
Neither; caches only help with linked data structures
questions.explain: C is row-major, so with `j` innermost consecutive accesses are 4 bytes apart and every fetched line is fully used. With `i` innermost each access is 4000 bytes after the last, touching a new line every time. Same big-O, very different constant.

questions.prompt: You read 1024 contiguous `int`s (4 bytes each) starting at a 64-byte-aligned address. How many distinct 64-byte cache lines do you touch?
questions.explain: 1024 * 4 = 4096 bytes, and 4096 / 64 = 64 lines. Each line holds 16 ints, so 15 of every 16 reads hit in the cache after the first. 1024 would be the count if every int needed its own line, which is what a random access pattern approaches.

questions.prompt: Summing 10 million values is about 10x faster from an array than from a linked list whose nodes were allocated in random order, though both are O(n). What explains most of the gap?
options: The list does more arithmetic per element
Array traversal is sequential, so lines are fully used and prefetched; each list node is a dependent load to an unpredictable address, often a ~100 ns miss
Arrays live on the stack and lists on the heap
The compiler cannot add numbers stored in structs
questions.explain: The list cannot even start loading node k+1 until node k arrives (the address is inside it), so misses serialise; the array's addresses are known in advance and the prefetcher streams them. Where the memory lives is irrelevant: a heap array is just as fast. Big-O from your DSA course counts operations, not cache misses.

lessons.title: Virtual memory and paging
lessons.objective: By the end you can split a virtual address into page number and offset, translate it through a page table, and explain what happens on a page fault.
concept: Every pointer your program uses is a **virtual address**. The **MMU** (memory management unit) in the CPU translates each one to a **physical address** in RAM on every access. Memory is managed in fixed-size **pages**: 4 KiB on x86-64 Linux (16 KiB on Apple Silicon). With 4 KiB pages, the low 12 bits of an address are the **offset** within the page and the remaining high bits are the **virtual page number (VPN)**. Translation replaces the VPN with a **physical frame number (PFN)** and keeps the offset.

The mapping lives in a per-process **page table**, maintained by the kernel. Each entry holds the PFN plus bits: present, writable, user-accessible, accessed, dirty. A flat table for 48-bit addresses would need 2^36 entries, so x86-64 uses a **4-level tree** (9 bits of the VPN per level, 512 entries per 4 KiB table page) and only allocates the parts that are used. Switching processes means pointing the MMU at a different root (the `CR3` register on x86).

When an entry is not present, the CPU raises a **page fault** and the kernel decides. A **minor** fault is cheap: first touch of freshly `malloc`ed memory gets a zero-filled frame. A **major** fault reads the page from disk (swap or a memory-mapped file) and costs milliseconds. An access with no valid mapping, or a write to a read-only page, becomes **SIGSEGV**. Virtual memory buys isolation (you cannot name another process's memory), lazy allocation, shared libraries mapped once into many processes, and copy-on-write `fork`.

items.label: Split
items.detail: VPN = 0x403 (bits 12 and up), offset = 0xABC (low 12 bits)

items.label: Page table lookup
items.detail: entry[0x403] = { present, writable, PFN 0x1F2 }

items.label: Combine
items.detail: physical = (0x1F2 << 12) | 0xABC = 0x1F2ABC

items.label: If not present
items.detail: page fault: kernel maps a frame (or sends SIGSEGV), then retries

example.code:
PAGE = 4096                      # 2**12, so 12 offset bits
page_table = {0x403: 0x1F2, 0x404: 0x0A7}   # VPN -> PFN

def translate(va):
    vpn, offset = va >> 12, va & 0xFFF
    if vpn not in page_table:
        raise MemoryError(f'page fault at {va:#x}')
    return (page_table[vpn] << 12) | offset

print(hex(translate(0x403ABC)))   # 0x1f2abc
print(hex(translate(0x404000)))   # 0xa7000
example.explain: This is the MMU's job in four lines: shift and mask to split the address, look up the frame, glue the offset back on. Contiguous virtual pages (0x403, 0x404) can map to frames anywhere in RAM, which is why the kernel never needs to find large contiguous physical regions.

Then on Linux run `/usr/bin/time -v python3 -c "bytearray(500_000_000)"` (or on macOS `/usr/bin/time -l`) and find the page-fault count. Explain the number.

questions.prompt: What does the MMU do?
options: Translates virtual addresses to physical addresses on every memory access
Moves pages between RAM and disk
questions.explain: The MMU is hardware that walks (or caches) the page table on each access. Moving pages to and from disk and handling faults is the kernel's software job, `malloc` is a library, and scheduling is the kernel's scheduler.

questions.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, what does this Python print?

va = 0x12345678
print(hex(va >> 12), hex(va & 0xFFF))
questions.explain: 4 KiB = 2^12, so the offset is the low 12 bits (3 hex digits: 0x678) and the page number is what remains after shifting them off (0x12345). Every hex digit is 4 bits, which is why page boundaries are easy to read in hex.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit system uses 4 KiB pages and a single-level page table with 4-byte entries. How big is one process's page table?
questions.explain: 32 - 12 = 20 bits of page number, so 2^20 entries, each 4 bytes: 4 MiB per process, even for a tiny program. That waste is why real systems use multi-level tables that allocate only the used parts.

questions.prompt: On a machine with 8 GiB of RAM and no swap, `char *p = malloc(10UL << 30)` (10 GiB) returns non-NULL on Linux with default settings. Why?
options: The kernel overcommits: it reserves virtual address space and only assigns physical frames when each page is first touched
malloc stores the excess on the stack
questions.explain: Allocating creates mappings, not frames. Each page gets a physical frame on its first access, through a minor page fault. If you then actually write all 10 GiB, the kernel runs out of frames and the OOM killer terminates a process. That is why a successful `malloc` is not a promise of physical memory.

A fixed-size block, usually 4 KiB; an address is page number plus offset.
The per-process map from virtual page numbers to physical frames.
Raised when a page isn't present; the kernel maps it or kills the process.

mistakes.right: It's virtual. The same address in two processes maps to different physical memory.

mistakes.right: Most are normal: first touch of new memory or loading a page of a file. Only invalid accesses become `SIGSEGV`.

lessons.title: The TLB: making translation fast
lessons.objective: By the end you can compute TLB reach, estimate the cost of TLB misses, and explain when huge pages help.
concept: A 4-level page table means a translation could cost four extra memory accesses before the real one. That would make every load five times slower, so the CPU caches recent translations in the **TLB** (translation lookaside buffer). A typical core has an L1 data TLB of about 64 entries and a unified L2 TLB of about 1,500-2,000 entries. A TLB hit costs essentially nothing; a miss triggers a hardware **page walk** that takes tens of cycles if the page-table entries are in cache, and hundreds if they are not.

**TLB reach** is how much memory the TLB can map at once: entries times page size. 64 entries of 4 KiB cover only 256 KiB; 1,536 entries cover 6 MiB. A program whose working set is a few GiB, accessed randomly, misses in the TLB on most accesses, on top of missing in the cache. **Huge pages** (2 MiB, or 1 GiB on x86-64) multiply reach by 512 per entry, which is why databases and JVMs enable them.

Context switches complicate things: entries belong to one address space. Older CPUs flushed the TLB on every switch; modern ones tag entries with an address-space ID (PCID on x86, ASID on ARM) so entries survive. When the kernel changes a mapping, for example after `munmap`, it must invalidate stale entries on every core that might cache them (a **TLB shootdown**), which is one reason unmapping memory is expensive.

steps.label: CPU issues VA
steps.detail: A load instruction computes virtual address 0x7f3a12c4

steps.label: TLB lookup
steps.detail: Hit: physical address in about a cycle, done

steps.label: Page walk
steps.detail: Miss: hardware reads up to 4 page-table levels from cache or RAM

steps.label: Fill TLB

steps.label: Access cache/RAM

steps.label: Or fault

example.code:
def reach(entries, page_bytes):
    return entries * page_bytes

KiB, MiB = 1024, 1024 ** 2
print(reach(64, 4 * KiB) // KiB, 'KiB')      # 256 KiB with 4 KiB pages
print(reach(64, 2 * MiB) // MiB, 'MiB')      # 128 MiB with 2 MiB pages

# average translation cost: hit rate h, hit cost 1 cycle, miss adds a 30-cycle walk
for h in (0.99, 0.90):
    print(h, round(1 + (1 - h) * 30, 2))      # 1.3 and 4.0 cycles
example.explain: Huge pages give the same 64 entries 512 times the reach. The cost model shows why hit rate dominates: dropping from 99% to 90% hits roughly triples the average translation cost.

lessons.tryit: Write a C program that allocates 1 GiB and reads one byte from every 4096-byte page, in sequential order and then in a shuffled order of page indexes; time both. Then repeat with a stride of 64 bytes inside a 256 KiB buffer. Explain which run is limited by TLB misses and which is not.

questions.prompt: What does the TLB cache?
questions.explain: The TLB caches page-table entries (VPN to PFN plus permission bits). Data and instructions are cached by the L1/L2/L3 caches, and recently used file data lives in the kernel's page cache.

questions.prompt: What does this Python print? (TLB reach in KiB with 4 KiB pages, then in MiB with 2 MiB pages.)

entries = 1536
print(entries * 4, entries * 2)
questions.explain: Reach = entries * page size: 1536 * 4 KiB = 6144 KiB (6 MiB) and 1536 * 2 MiB = 3072 MiB (3 GiB). Huge pages let the same TLB cover a multi-gigabyte working set.

questions.prompt: TLB hit rate is 99%, a hit adds 1 cycle and a miss adds a 30-cycle page walk on top. What is the average translation cost?
questions.explain: Every access pays the 1-cycle lookup and 1% pay 30 more: 1 + 0.01 * 30 = 1.3. The cost model is the same as for data caches: average = hit time + miss rate * miss penalty.

questions.prompt: A loop reads one byte from each 4 KiB page of a 1 GiB array, visiting pages in random order. It touches only 256 Ki bytes in total, yet runs far slower than reading 256 KiB contiguously. Why?
options: Reading single bytes is slower than reading ints
Each access is on a different page, so nearly every one misses in both the TLB (reach is a few MiB) and the cache, paying a page walk plus a DRAM access
The OS zeroes each page on every read
Random numbers are slow to generate
questions.explain: The contiguous 256 KiB fits in about 64 pages and 4096 cache lines that are prefetched in order. The random version needs 262,144 distinct pages and lines with no pattern, so each access is a TLB miss plus a cache miss. Huge pages would fix the TLB half; a better data layout fixes both.

video.title: Pages, Page Tables, MMU & TLB & Address Translation Explained

lessons.why: Large-memory programs can spend much of their time on address translation. Understanding the TLB explains when huge pages and better locality pay off.

terms.d: A small cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.
Reading the page table levels after a TLB miss.
Entries × page size: how much memory the TLB can map at once.
2 MiB or 1 GiB pages that multiply TLB reach.

mistakes.wrong: Address translation is free.
mistakes.right: A TLB miss means a page walk of up to four memory accesses.

mistakes.wrong: Huge pages always help.
mistakes.right: They help large, randomly accessed working sets; they waste memory for small or sparse ones.

takeaways: 64 entries × 4 KiB covers only 256 KiB.
Random access across gigabytes causes constant TLB misses.
Address-space IDs avoid flushing the TLB on every context switch.

lessons.title: Inside malloc: writing a simple allocator
lessons.objective: By the end you can design a heap allocator with block headers, a free list, splitting and coalescing, and explain the fragmentation trade-offs of its placement policy.
concept: `malloc` is ordinary C code. It gets large regions from the kernel (with `sbrk` or `mmap`) and carves them into **blocks**. Each block starts with a **header** recording its size and whether it is allocated; `malloc` returns the address just past the header, and `free(p)` finds the header at `p - sizeof(header)`. Payloads are **aligned** to 16 bytes on 64-bit systems, so sizes are multiples of 16 and the low 4 bits of the size field are free to store flags such as the allocated bit.

Free blocks are tracked in a **free list**. An **implicit** list walks every block by adding sizes; an **explicit** list threads `next`/`prev` pointers through the payloads of free blocks only, which is faster. To satisfy a request, a **placement policy** chooses a block: **first fit** (first big enough), **next fit** (resume where the last search stopped), or **best fit** (smallest big enough, slower but less waste). If the chosen block is much larger than needed, **split** it and return the remainder to the list.

On `free`, **coalesce** the block with free neighbours, or the heap shatters into slivers. A **footer** (a copy of the header at the block's end, a 'boundary tag') lets you find the previous block in O(1). Waste comes in two kinds: **internal fragmentation** (padding and headers inside allocated blocks) and **external fragmentation** (enough free bytes in total, but no single block big enough). Production allocators (glibc's ptmalloc, jemalloc, mimalloc) use **segregated lists** by size class and per-thread caches.

items.label: Header 32|1
items.detail: allocated block: 8-byte header, 24-byte payload (with padding)

items.label: Header 48|0
items.detail: free block: payload holds next/prev free-list pointers

items.label: Header 16|1
items.detail: allocated block: smallest useful size

items.label: Header 64|0

example.explain: `ALIGN16` rounds up by adding 15 and clearing the low 4 bits. The bump allocator is what arenas and per-frame game allocators really use: allocation is an add and a compare. Your project replaces `top` with headers and a free list so that memory can be reused.

lessons.tryit: Extend the bump allocator: give every block an 8-byte header storing `size | allocated`, make `my_free` mark the block free, and make `my_malloc` first walk the blocks looking for a free one that fits (implicit free list, first fit). Draw the heap after `a = my_malloc(10); b = my_malloc(40); my_free(a); c = my_malloc(8);` before running it, then print the heap to check.

questions.prompt: What is external fragmentation?
options: Free memory that exists in total but is split into blocks too small for a request
Memory leaked because the program never called free
Memory used by the allocator's headers
questions.explain: External fragmentation is about the gaps between allocated blocks. Padding and header overhead inside blocks is internal fragmentation, and leaks are a bug in the program, not a property of the allocator.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: Adding 15 then clearing the low 4 bits rounds up to the next multiple of 16: 1 -> 16, 16 stays 16 (31 rounds down to 16), 17 -> 32. Casting to `size_t` before `~` matters: `~15` as an `int` would also work here through sign extension, but `~15u` (32-bit) would clear the upper half of a 64-bit size.

questions.prompt: The free list holds blocks of 40, 16 and 24 bytes, in that order. A request needs 20 bytes. Which block does best fit choose, and which does first fit choose?
questions.explain: First fit takes the first block that is large enough: 40. Best fit searches for the smallest block that still fits: 24 (16 is too small). Best fit leaves a 4-byte sliver instead of a 20-byte one, at the cost of scanning the whole list.

questions.prompt: Your allocator never coalesces. A program allocates two adjacent 32-byte blocks, frees both, then asks for 48 bytes, and the allocator must grow the heap even though 64 free bytes sit side by side. What is the problem and the fix?
options: External fragmentation caused by not merging neighbours; coalesce adjacent free blocks on free, using boundary-tag footers to find the previous block
A memory leak; call free twice
questions.explain: Two separate 32-byte free blocks cannot satisfy 48 bytes, though together they could. Coalescing on free merges them into one 64-byte block. With a footer at the end of each block, `free` can find and check both neighbours in constant time.

video.title: Coding a Memory Allocator From Scratch

lessons.why: Writing an allocator shows exactly what `malloc` and `free` cost, why fragmentation happens and why memory bugs corrupt the heap so badly.

terms.d: Size and allocated bit stored just before each block's payload.
A list of free blocks: implicit (walk all blocks) or explicit (linked free blocks).
Cut a large free block to fit a request / merge adjacent free blocks.
Internal: waste inside blocks. External: free memory too scattered to use.

mistakes.wrong: `free(p)` only needs the pointer, so the allocator must search for the block size.
mistakes.right: The size is in the header right before `p`, which is why writing before a buffer corrupts the heap.

mistakes.wrong: Best fit always beats first fit.
mistakes.right: Best fit can leave tiny unusable slivers and costs more to search. Each placement policy trades speed for fragmentation.

takeaways: Headers make `free` O(1) to find the block size.
Coalescing with boundary tags prevents the heap from shattering.
Segregated free lists by size are what real allocators use.

project.title: Your own malloc with free lists
project.brief: Write `mymalloc.c` providing `my_malloc`, `my_free`, `my_calloc` and `my_realloc` on top of memory obtained with `mmap` (or `sbrk`), using block headers, an explicit free list, splitting and coalescing. It makes headers, alignment, fragmentation and the stack/heap distinction concrete, and you can measure your locality and fragmentation choices.
milestones: Get memory from the OS with `mmap`, and implement a bump allocator that passes a test of 10,000 random-size allocations with 16-byte alignment checked via `(uintptr_t)p % 16 == 0`.
Add headers (size | allocated bit) and an implicit free list with first fit, so freed blocks are reused.
Add splitting of oversized blocks and coalescing with the next and previous free blocks using footers.
Switch to an explicit doubly linked free list; print a heap dump function's output after a scripted sequence and compare it with a hand-drawn diagram.
Implement `my_realloc` (grow in place if the next block is free, else allocate-copy-free) and `my_calloc`.
Benchmark against the system malloc on a trace of 1 million operations: report time and peak heap size, and explain any difference.
project.stretch: Add segregated free lists by size class (16, 32, 64, ... bytes) and measure the speedup on a workload dominated by small allocations; on Linux, load your allocator into a real program with `LD_PRELOAD`.

exam.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, which virtual page number and offset does address 0x7f002ab8 have?
exam.explain: 4 KiB = 2^12, so the offset is the low 12 bits, the last 3 hex digits (0xab8), and the VPN is everything above (0x7f002). Splitting at 4 hex digits would be 64 KiB pages, at 2 digits 256-byte pages.

exam.prompt: `int a[4][8];` with 4-byte ints. How many bytes past the start of `a` is `a[2][3]`?
exam.explain: Row-major layout: element index = 2 * 8 + 3 = 19, and each element is 4 bytes, so 76. 19 forgets to multiply by the element size, 20 just adds the indexes, and 56 is the column-major answer ((3 * 4 + 2) * 4), which is Fortran's layout, not C's.

exam.prompt: A particle system stores `struct particle { float x, y, z, vx, vy, vz; char name[40]; }` (64 bytes) in an array, and the hot loop only reads `x` for every particle. Splitting it into separate arrays `float xs[N], ys[N], ...` makes the loop about 10x faster. Why?
options: Separate arrays use less total memory
With the struct array each 64-byte line yields one useful 4-byte `x`; with `xs[]` every line holds 16 useful values, so the loop moves 16x less data from memory
Floats in structs cannot be vectorised
Arrays of structs are allocated on the stack
exam.explain: This is array-of-structs versus struct-of-arrays. Memory bandwidth and misses scale with lines fetched, not values used. Total memory is the same either way; the win is that the loop's working set shrinks from 64 bytes per particle to 4.

exam.prompt: Roughly how long does one access to main memory (DRAM) take on a modern desktop CPU, as a cache miss?
exam.explain: DRAM is about 100 ns, roughly 100x an L1 hit (~1 ns). ~100 us is an SSD read and ~10 ms a spinning-disk seek. At 4 GHz, 100 ns is about 400 cycles the core may spend waiting.

exam.prompt: Which access produces a SIGSEGV rather than a page fault the kernel silently resolves?
options: First write to a page of a freshly malloc'd 1 MiB buffer
Reading a page of a memory-mapped file that is not yet in RAM
Writing to a string literal, which lives in a read-only page
First touch of a new stack page just below the current stack pointer, within the stack limit
exam.explain: All four cause a page fault. In the first, second and fourth the kernel finds a valid mapping that is just not populated yet, maps a frame and resumes (minor or major fault). A write to a page mapped read-only is a protection violation, so the kernel delivers SIGSEGV.

exam.prompt: In your allocator, sizes are multiples of 16 and bit 0 of the header is the allocated flag. A header reads 0x31. What does it describe?
exam.explain: 0x31 = 0b0011_0001. Mask off the low 4 flag bits (`h & ~0xF`) to get 0x30 = 48; bit 0 is 1, so it is allocated. Sizes are never odd, which is exactly why the low bits can be borrowed for flags.

exam.prompt: Connecting to DSA: a hash table with separate chaining (a linked list per bucket) and one with open addressing (linear probing in a flat array) both have O(1) expected lookups. Why is open addressing usually faster in practice at moderate load factors?
options: Probes walk adjacent slots in one array, often in the same cache line, while chaining follows pointers to separately allocated nodes that each risk a cache miss
exam.explain: Both resolve collisions, and linear probing actually has more of them. The difference is memory behaviour: a probe sequence is sequential memory that the cache and prefetcher love, while each chain hop is a dependent pointer load to a random heap address. Open addressing does need resizing, and must keep the load factor low.

exam.prompt: A CPU has a 64-entry L1 data TLB and uses 4 KiB pages. What is its reach?
exam.explain: Reach = entries * page size = 64 * 4 KiB = 256 KiB. A working set bigger than that, accessed randomly, starts missing in the L1 TLB even when the data itself is cached in L2 or L3.

modules.title: Operating systems
modules.summary: How the kernel virtualises the machine: processes and fork/exec/wait, system calls, scheduling, files and descriptors, pipes and signals.

lessons.title: Processes: fork, exec, wait
lessons.objective: By the end you can write C that starts another program the way a shell does, and predict what parent and child each see after `fork`.
concept: A **process** is a running program: an address space, registers including the PC, a table of open files, and an ID (PID). Unix creates processes with an odd but powerful pair of calls. `fork()` clones the calling process: the child gets a copy of the parent's memory, open files and PC, so both continue from the same line. The only difference is the return value: `0` in the child, the child's PID in the parent, `-1` on failure.

`exec` (`execvp`, `execve`, ...) replaces the current process's program with a new one: new code, fresh stack and heap, same PID and the same open files. It does not return on success, so any line after it runs only on error. The split is the point: between `fork` and `exec`, the child can rearrange its own file descriptors, working directory or environment, which is exactly how shells implement redirection and pipes without the new program knowing.

`waitpid(pid, &status, 0)` blocks the parent until that child exits, then `WIFEXITED(status)` and `WEXITSTATUS(status)` decode how it ended. A child that has exited but not yet been waited for is a **zombie**: it holds only its PID and exit status, waiting to be reaped. If the parent dies first, the orphan is adopted by PID 1 (init or launchd), which reaps it. A shell is a loop of read a line, `fork`, `exec` in the child, `waitpid` in the parent.
