steps.detail: Shell reads 'ls -l' and splits it into argv

steps.label: fork()
steps.detail: Kernel clones the shell; child gets 0, parent gets the child PID

steps.label: Child: execvp
steps.detail: Child replaces itself with /bin/ls; same PID, same fds

steps.label: ls runs
steps.detail: Writes to fd 1 (inherited terminal), then exit(0)

steps.label: Parent: waitpid
steps.detail: Shell blocks, reaps the child, reads exit status 0

steps.label: Prompt
steps.detail: Shell prints the next prompt and loops

example.explain: The child becomes `echo`, prints, and exits; the parent waits and decodes the status. `_exit(127)` after a failed exec is the shell convention for 'command not found', and `_exit` (not `exit`) avoids flushing a copy of the parent's stdio buffers twice.

lessons.tryit: Write `run.c` that takes a command on its command line (`./run ls -l /tmp`), forks, execs it with `execvp(argv[1], &argv[1])`, waits, and prints the exit status. Test it with a command that succeeds, one that fails (`ls /nope`), and one that does not exist. Then make the child `sleep 30` and run `ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm` from another terminal before and after the child exits without being waited for (comment out `waitpid` and add a `sleep(60)` in the parent) to see a zombie (`Z`).

questions.prompt: What does `fork()` return in the child process?
questions.explain: The child gets 0 and the parent gets the child's PID; that difference is how the same code takes two paths. -1 means fork failed, and a child that wants its parent's PID calls `getppid()`.

questions.prompt: What does the parent print?
questions.explain: After `fork` the child has its own copy of the address space (copy-on-write under the hood). Changing `x` in the child writes to the child's copy only, so the parent still sees 1, even though the variable has the same virtual address in both processes.

questions.prompt: How many times does this program print `hi`?
questions.explain: The first `fork` makes 2 processes; each of them runs the second `fork`, making 4; all 4 run the `printf`. In general, n sequential forks yield 2^n processes. The order of the lines is not deterministic, but the count is.

questions.prompt: `printf("hello\n"); fork(); return 0;` prints `hello` once in a terminal but twice when run as `./prog > out.txt`. Why?
options: The kernel duplicates the write when stdout is a file
stdout is line-buffered for a terminal (flushed at the newline) but fully buffered for a file, so 'hello' is still in the buffer at fork and both processes flush their copy at exit
fork re-executes the program from the start when output is redirected
Files do not support the newline character
questions.explain: `fork` copies user memory, including stdio's unflushed buffer. On a terminal the newline flushed it before the fork; to a file nothing was written yet, so parent and child each write 'hello' when they exit. Call `fflush(stdout)` before `fork` (and use `_exit` in children) to avoid it.

video.title: fork(), exec(), wait() - How UNIX Really Creates Processes

lessons.why: Every shell, server and build tool starts programs this way. `fork`, `exec` and `wait` are the core of how Unix runs anything.

terms.d: A running program: address space, registers, open files and a PID.
Clones the process; returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent.
Replaces the current program with a new one, keeping the PID and open files.
A child that has exited but hasn't been waited for yet.

mistakes.wrong: Code after a successful `exec` call still runs.
mistakes.right: `exec` doesn't return on success; only error-handling code after it ever runs.

mistakes.wrong: After `fork`, parent and child share variables.
mistakes.right: Each gets its own copy of the address space; changes in one aren't seen by the other.

takeaways: A shell forks, the child execs the command, the parent waits.
Check `fork`'s return value to know which process you're in.
Always `waitpid` for children to avoid zombies.

lessons.title: System calls: crossing into the kernel
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how a system call transfers control to the kernel, tell syscalls from library functions, and handle their errors with `errno`.
concept: User programs run in **user mode**, where the CPU forbids privileged instructions and access to kernel memory. To do anything involving hardware or other processes (read a file, send a packet, start a process), a program asks the kernel through a **system call**. It places a syscall number and arguments in registers and executes a trap instruction (`syscall` on x86-64, `svc` on ARM64). The CPU switches to **kernel mode** and jumps to a fixed entry point the kernel registered at boot.

The kernel validates every argument (a pointer must be in your address space, a file descriptor must be yours), does the work, places the result in a register, and returns to user mode just after the trap. A syscall costs roughly 100 ns to a few microseconds, versus about 1 ns for a function call, so programs **batch**: `printf` and `fwrite` collect bytes in a user-space buffer and call `write` once per few KiB.

Most of what you call 'system calls' are thin **libc wrappers** (`read`, `write`, `open`, `fork`); `printf`, `strlen` and `malloc` are ordinary library functions (malloc occasionally calls `mmap` or `brk`). Syscalls report failure by returning -1 and setting the thread-local `errno` (`ENOENT`, `EACCES`, `EINTR`...); `perror("open")` or `strerror(errno)` turns it into text. Watch any program's syscalls with `strace ./prog` on Linux or `sudo dtruss ./prog` on macOS.

steps.label: User code
steps.detail: Calls the libc wrapper write()

steps.label: Wrapper
steps.detail: Puts syscall number and args (fd, buf, len) in registers

steps.label: Trap
steps.detail: syscall / svc: CPU switches to kernel mode at the kernel entry

steps.label: Kernel
steps.detail: Checks fd 1 and the buffer, copies bytes to the terminal or pipe

steps.label: Return
steps.detail: Result (3) in a register, back to user mode; -1 sets errno

example.explain: `write` goes straight to the kernel. `open` fails with `ENOENT` (2 on Linux and macOS), which `strerror` and `perror` translate. Always check the return value: syscalls fail for reasons outside your control, such as permissions, full disks or interrupted calls.

lessons.tryit: Run `strace -c ls` (Linux) or `sudo dtruss -c ls` (macOS) and list the three most frequent syscalls. Then write two programs that output one million bytes, one calling `write(1, &c, 1)` per byte and one using `putchar`; time both with output to `/dev/null` and count their syscalls. Explain the ratio.

questions.prompt: What is a system call?
options: A call to any function in the C standard library
A controlled transfer from user mode into the kernel to request a privileged service
A function that runs in a separate thread
An interrupt sent by a device to the CPU
questions.explain: A syscall is a deliberate trap into the kernel. Many libc functions never make one (`strlen`, `qsort`), and device interrupts are asynchronous hardware events, not requests from your program.

questions.prompt: What does this print? (Note the length argument.)
questions.explain: `write` sends exactly the number of bytes you ask for, 3 here: `hel`, with no newline. It returns the count written, which `printf` then prints followed by a newline. The kernel does not know or care that the buffer holds a C string.

questions.prompt: `open("missing.txt", O_RDONLY)` returns -1. What is the idiomatic way to report why?
options: Call `perror("open")`, which prints the message for the current `errno` (here 'No such file or directory')
questions.explain: Syscalls signal failure with -1 and put the reason in `errno` (`ENOENT` here). `perror` formats it. Retrying makes sense only for transient errors such as `EINTR`, and `ferror` is for stdio streams, not raw file descriptors. Read `errno` immediately, before another call overwrites it.

questions.prompt: Writing a 1 MB file one byte at a time with `write()` takes about a second; using `fputc` takes a few milliseconds. What explains the difference?
options: `write` makes one syscall per byte (a million mode switches); `fputc` fills a user-space buffer and calls `write` once per few KiB, a few hundred syscalls total
`fputc` writes to memory and never to the disk
The kernel throttles programs that use `write` directly
questions.explain: Both end up in the same kernel `write`; the cost is per call, not per byte. A million crossings at ~1 us each is about a second. Buffering amortises the crossing, and `fputc`'s data does reach the file when the buffer is flushed, at the latest at `fclose` or exit.

video.title: How Operating Systems Actually Work (kernel mode vs. user mode)

lessons.why: Every file, network and process operation goes through system calls. Knowing their cost and error rules explains performance and robustness of real programs.

terms.d: Restricted mode for programs; privileged mode for the OS.
A controlled jump into the kernel to request a service.
The C function (`read`, `write`) that issues the syscall.
Set on failure to say why; check the return value first.

mistakes.wrong: `printf` and `malloc` are system calls.
mistakes.right: They're library functions that sometimes make system calls (`write`, `mmap`).

mistakes.wrong: I can check `errno` to see if a call failed.
mistakes.right: `errno` is only meaningful after a call reports failure, usually by returning -1.

takeaways: Syscalls cross into kernel mode and back, costing far more than a function call.
Batch work to reduce the number of syscalls.
Check every return value, then read `errno` with `perror` or `strerror`.

lessons.title: CPU scheduling
lessons.objective: By the end you can compute turnaround and response times for FIFO, SJF and Round Robin by hand and explain what a real scheduler optimises for.
concept: With more runnable threads than cores, the OS **time-shares**: run one for a while, then switch. A hardware **timer interrupt** fires every few milliseconds and hands control to the kernel even if the running program never makes a syscall; that is **preemption**. A **context switch** saves the registers of the old thread, loads the new one's, and possibly switches page tables. It costs a few microseconds directly and more indirectly, because the new thread starts with cold caches and TLB.

Two metrics pull in different directions. **Turnaround time** is completion minus arrival; **response time** is first run minus arrival. **FIFO** suffers the **convoy effect**: a long job in front makes every short job wait. **Shortest Job First** (or its preemptive version, STCF) minimises average turnaround, but needs to know job lengths. **Round Robin** gives each job a time slice in turn, which is great for response time and poor for turnaround.

Real schedulers cannot see the future, so they learn from behaviour. **MLFQ** (multi-level feedback queue) demotes jobs that use their whole slice (CPU-bound) and keeps jobs that block quickly (interactive, I/O-bound) at high priority. Linux's CFS, and since 6.6 EEVDF, tracks each thread's weighted CPU time (`vruntime`) and runs whoever has had the least, with `nice` values adjusting the weights. Shorter slices improve responsiveness but increase switching overhead.

visual.title: Scheduling policies at a glance
rows: needs job lengths; long jobs starve

example.code:
def fifo(jobs):           # jobs: run times, all arriving at t=0
    t, total = 0, 0
    for j in jobs:
        t += j                # job finishes at time t
        total += t
    return total / len(jobs)

jobs = [10, 1, 1]
print(fifo(jobs))          # 11.0  (finish at 10, 11, 12)
print(fifo(sorted(jobs)))  # 5.0   (SJF: finish at 1, 2, 12)
example.explain: Same jobs, same total work, very different average turnaround: running the long job first makes both short jobs wait 10 units. Sorting by length is exactly SJF when all jobs arrive together.

lessons.tryit: Extend the example with a Round Robin simulator (time slice q) that reports average turnaround and average response time. Run jobs [10, 1, 1] with q = 1 and q = 5 and compare with FIFO and SJF in a small table. Then run `yes > /dev/null &` four times on your machine, watch `top`, and kill them; explain what the scheduler did.

questions.prompt: What lets the OS take the CPU away from a program stuck in an infinite loop that makes no syscalls?
options: A periodic hardware timer interrupt that transfers control to the kernel
questions.explain: The kernel programs a timer at boot; each tick traps into the kernel, which can then decide to switch threads. Without it, a cooperative system would have to wait for the program to give up the CPU voluntarily, which an infinite loop never does.

questions.prompt: Jobs all arrive at t=0. What does this SJF calculation print?
questions.code:
jobs = [3, 1, 2]
t = total = 0
for j in sorted(jobs):
    t += j
    total += t
print(total)
questions.explain: Sorted order is 1, 2, 3, finishing at t = 1, 3 and 6. The turnaround times sum to 1 + 3 + 6 = 10 (an average of 3.33). FIFO in the given order would finish at 3, 4, 6, summing to 13.

questions.prompt: Jobs A (100 ms), B (10 ms) and C (10 ms) arrive at t=0 in that order. Under FIFO, what is the average turnaround time?
questions.explain: A finishes at 100, B at 110, C at 120: (100 + 110 + 120) / 3 = 110 ms. Running B and C first (SJF) gives (10 + 20 + 120) / 3 = 50 ms. That gap is the convoy effect.

questions.prompt: Why don't schedulers use a tiny time slice such as 10 microseconds to make everything feel responsive?
options: Each switch costs microseconds directly plus cold caches and TLB afterwards, so a large fraction of CPU time would go to switching instead of work
Shorter slices increase turnaround of short jobs
Programs would crash if interrupted that often
questions.explain: If a switch costs ~5 us including cache warm-up, a 10 us slice spends about a third of the time on overhead. Slices of a few milliseconds keep overhead around 0.1%. The trade-off between responsiveness and throughput is the central tuning knob.

video.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms: FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, Priority

lessons.why: Schedulers decide what runs when, which is why your UI stays responsive while a compile runs. The trade-offs carry over to job queues and load balancers.

terms.d: Completion time minus arrival time.
First-run time minus arrival time.
Give each job a time slice in turn: good response, worse turnaround.
Multi-level feedback queue: learns which jobs are interactive from their behaviour.

mistakes.wrong: One scheduling policy is best for everything.
mistakes.right: SJF minimises turnaround, Round Robin minimises response time; they pull in opposite directions.

mistakes.wrong: A smaller time slice is always better.
mistakes.right: Each context switch has a cost, so very small slices waste time switching.

takeaways: FIFO suffers the convoy effect behind long jobs.
Preemption via timer interrupts keeps one job from hogging the CPU.
Real schedulers infer job types from behaviour.

lessons.title: Files, inodes and file descriptors
lessons.objective: By the end you can trace a file descriptor through the kernel's tables to the inode, use `dup2` to redirect output, and explain links and deletion.
concept: A **file descriptor** is a small integer index into your process's **fd table**. Each entry points to an **open file description** in the kernel holding the current **offset** and the flags it was opened with, which in turn points to the file's **inode**. By convention fd 0 is stdin, 1 is stdout and 2 is stderr. `open` always returns the **lowest unused** fd number, `read` and `write` move the offset, and `lseek` sets it.

`dup2(old, new)` makes fd `new` point to the same open file description as `old`, closing `new` first if needed. That is all shell redirection is: for `prog > out.txt`, the shell's child opens `out.txt` (say as fd 3), calls `dup2(3, 1)`, closes 3, and execs `prog`, which writes to fd 1 as usual without knowing. After `fork`, parent and child share open file descriptions, including the offset.

An **inode** stores a file's metadata (size, owner, permissions, timestamps) and where its data blocks are, but not its name. A **directory** is a table mapping names to inode numbers. A **hard link** (`ln a b`) is a second name for the same inode; `rm` is really `unlink`, which removes a name and decrements the link count. The data is freed only when the link count is 0 and no process has it open. `write` returning does not mean data is on disk; `fsync` forces it.

questions.prompt: Which file descriptor is standard error by convention?
questions.explain: 0 is stdin, 1 is stdout, 2 is stderr. The first file your program opens is usually 3, because 0-2 are already taken.

questions.prompt: Assume fds 0, 1 and 2 are open when the program starts. What does it print?
questions.explain: `open` returns the lowest-numbered unused descriptor, and closing 0 freed it. Old shells implemented `< file` exactly this way (close 0, then open) before `dup2` existed.

questions.prompt: In a shell: `echo hi > a; ln a b; rm a; cat b`. What happens?
options: `cat` fails: No such file or directory
It prints nothing, because the data was deleted
`ln` fails because `a` is not a directory
questions.explain: `ln` creates a second directory entry for the same inode (link count 2). `rm a` removes one name (link count 1), so the inode and data remain, reachable as `b`. With a symbolic link (`ln -s`), `cat b` would fail, because a symlink stores a path, not an inode.

questions.prompt: A server's disk is full. You `rm` a 20 GB log file, but `df` shows no space freed. What is the most likely reason?
options: `rm` only moves files to the trash
The server process still has the log open; the inode and its blocks are freed only when the last open descriptor is closed
`df` caches its results for an hour
Log files are stored in RAM
questions.explain: Unlinking removed the name, but the open file description keeps the inode alive, and the process may still be writing to it. `lsof | grep deleted` finds it; restart the process or truncate it via `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>` on Linux. This is also why log rotation tells processes to reopen their files.

lessons.why: File descriptors underlie files, pipes, sockets and terminals. Understanding them explains redirection, why deleting an open file doesn't free space, and how links work.

Kernel object holding the offset and flags; can be shared by several fds.
Metadata and data block locations for a file, without its name.
Another directory entry pointing at the same inode.

mistakes.wrong: Deleting a file frees its space immediately.
mistakes.right: `unlink` removes a name. Space is freed only when no links and no open descriptors remain.

mistakes.wrong: A file's name is stored in its inode.
mistakes.right: Names live in directories, which map names to inode numbers.

takeaways: `open` returns the lowest unused fd number.
`dup2(old, new)` is how shells redirect output.
Hard links share an inode; symbolic links store a path.

lessons.title: Pipes and signals
lessons.objective: By the end you can connect two processes with a pipe the way a shell does for `a | b`, and install a safe signal handler.
concept: `pipe(fds)` creates a one-way kernel buffer and two descriptors: `fds[0]` is the read end and `fds[1]` the write end. Writes append to the buffer (64 KiB on Linux) and block when it is full; reads block until data arrives, and return **0 (EOF)** only when the buffer is empty and *every* write end, in every process, is closed. Because descriptors survive `fork` and `exec`, a pipe created before forking connects parent and children.

For `ls | wc -l` a shell calls `pipe`, forks a child that does `dup2(fds[1], 1)` and execs `ls`, forks another that does `dup2(fds[0], 0)` and execs `wc`, and in every process closes the pipe fds it does not need, then waits for both. Forget to close a write end and `wc` never sees EOF and hangs forever. If the reader exits first, the writer gets **SIGPIPE**, whose default action kills it, which is how `yes | head -1` terminates.

A **signal** is an asynchronous notification delivered to a process: `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C), `SIGTERM` (polite kill), `SIGKILL` (cannot be caught or ignored), `SIGSEGV` (bad memory access), `SIGCHLD` (a child changed state), `SIGPIPE`. Install a handler with `sigaction`. A handler can interrupt your code anywhere, even inside `malloc`, so it may call only **async-signal-safe** functions (`write`, `_exit`, not `printf` or `malloc`). The safe pattern is to set a `volatile sig_atomic_t` flag and handle it in the main loop.

steps.detail: fds[0] = read end, fds[1] = write end

steps.label: fork child 1
steps.detail: dup2(fds[1], 1); close both fds; execvp("ls")

steps.label: fork child 2
steps.detail: dup2(fds[0], 0); close both fds; execvp("wc")

steps.label: Parent closes
steps.detail: close(fds[0]); close(fds[1]) so wc can see EOF

steps.detail: Reap both children; the pipeline's status is wc's

lessons.tryit: Write `pipeline.c` that runs the equivalent of `ls -l | wc -l` using `pipe`, two `fork`s, `dup2` and `execlp`, then waits for both children. Run it, then delete the parent's `close(fds[1])` and observe the hang; explain it with `ps` and `lsof -p <pid>` (or `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd` on Linux). Finally, add a SIGINT handler to your shell project skeleton so Ctrl-C does not kill the shell itself.

questions.prompt: Which signal can never be caught, blocked or ignored?
questions.explain: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) are handled by the kernel directly, so a stuck process can always be killed with `kill -9`. SIGINT and SIGTERM are commonly caught for clean shutdown, and SIGSEGV can be caught (for crash reporters), though returning from its handler usually just faults again.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: The 5 bytes written into the pipe sit in the kernel buffer; `read` asks for up to 16 and gets the 5 available (it does not wait for 16, because some data is ready). `%.*s` prints exactly `n` characters, which matters because the pipe does not add a terminating zero byte.

questions.prompt: Your shell runs `ls | wc -l`: `ls` exits, but `wc` never prints and never exits. The children close their unused pipe ends correctly. What did you most likely forget?
options: To close the parent's copy of the write end, `fds[1]`, so the write end stays open and `wc` never sees EOF
To flush stdout in the parent
questions.explain: `wc` reads until EOF, and EOF arrives only when every write end is closed. The parent still holds one from before the forks. Without the `dup2`, `ls` would have printed to the terminal and `wc` would still hang for the same reason. SIGPIPE goes to writers, not readers.

questions.prompt: Why does the safe signal-handler pattern set a `volatile sig_atomic_t` flag instead of calling `printf` inside the handler?
options: The handler can interrupt the program in the middle of `printf` or `malloc`, and re-entering them can deadlock or corrupt their internal state; only async-signal-safe functions may be called
Handlers cannot access global variables otherwise
questions.explain: stdio and malloc keep internal locks and buffers. If the signal lands while the main code holds that lock, a `printf` in the handler waits on itself forever or corrupts the buffer. `sig_atomic_t` writes are atomic with respect to signals, and `volatile` stops the compiler caching the flag in a register.

video.title: Pipes and Named Pipes in C

lessons.why: Pipes are how Unix tools combine, and signals are how processes are stopped, notified and cleaned up. Both appear in every long-running service.

terms.d: A one-way kernel buffer with a read end and a write end.
`read` returns 0 only when every write end is closed.
An asynchronous notification, such as `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`.
Functions safe to call inside a signal handler, like `write`; `printf` isn't.

mistakes.wrong: The reader gets EOF when the writer process finishes writing.
mistakes.right: Only when every copy of the write end is closed, including ones inherited by other processes.

mistakes.wrong: I can do anything in a signal handler.
mistakes.right: Handlers interrupt arbitrary code. Set a `volatile sig_atomic_t` flag or call async-signal-safe functions only.

takeaways: For `a | b`, each child `dup2`s one pipe end and closes all the others.
Unclosed write ends make readers hang forever.
Keep signal handlers tiny: set a flag and return.

project.title: A Unix shell with pipes and redirection
project.brief: Build `msh`, a shell that reads commands, runs them with `fork`/`execvp`/`waitpid`, and supports `<`, `>`, `>>`, pipelines of any length and the built-ins `cd` and `exit`. It is the canonical OS exercise because every feature is a direct use of this module's system calls.
milestones: Read a line with `getline`, split it into an argv array, run it with fork/execvp/waitpid, and print `msh: command not found` (exit status 127) on failure.
Implement the built-ins `cd` (with `chdir`) and `exit`, and explain in your README why `cd` cannot be an external program.
Implement `< file`, `> file` and `>> file` using `open` and `dup2` in the child before `exec`.
Implement two-stage pipelines `a | b`, closing every unused pipe end; verify that `ls | wc -l` and `yes | head -3` terminate.
Generalise to pipelines of N stages, and make the shell ignore SIGINT while children receive it (Ctrl-C kills `sleep 100`, not `msh`).
Store `$?` (the last exit status) and make `msh` reap background jobs started with `&`, leaving no zombies (check with `ps`).
project.stretch: Add job control: `jobs`, `fg` and `bg`, using process groups (`setpgid`), `tcsetpgrp` and SIGCHLD/SIGTSTP handling.

exam.prompt: Counting the original process, how many processes exist after this loop runs (assuming every fork succeeds)?
exam.explain: Each iteration doubles the number of processes, because every existing process (including children created in earlier iterations, which continue the loop) forks: 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8. Answering 4 counts only the forks made by the original process.

exam.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program runs `ls -l` in a child and waits for it.
exam.explain: Fork first, then branch on the child's return value of 0. The child execs; `_exit(127)` runs only if `exec` failed. The parent, which skips the block, waits for that child. Putting `waitpid` inside the block would make the child wait for itself.

exam.prompt: A long-running server forks a child per request and never calls `wait`. After a week, `ps` shows thousands of entries marked `Z` and new forks start failing. What is happening, and what is the fix?
options: Memory leak in the children; call `free` before exiting
Exited children remain as zombies holding PIDs until reaped; reap them with `waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG)` in a loop, for example triggered by SIGCHLD
The scheduler starves old processes; raise their priority
Children are stuck in infinite loops; send SIGKILL
exam.explain: A zombie has freed its memory but keeps its PID and exit status for the parent. With enough of them the PID or process limit is exhausted. Killing a zombie does nothing because it is already dead; only reaping (or the parent exiting, which makes init adopt and reap them) removes it.

exam.prompt: Why does `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` send both stdout and stderr to the file, while `cmd 2>&1 > out.txt` sends stderr to the terminal?
options: Bash parses redirections right to left
Redirections are applied left to right as `dup2` calls: `2>&1` copies whatever fd 1 refers to at that moment, the file in the first case and the terminal in the second
The second form is a syntax error that bash silently ignores
stderr cannot be redirected after stdout
exam.explain: `2>&1` means `dup2(1, 2)`: make fd 2 refer to what fd 1 refers to *now*. In the first command fd 1 is already the file; in the second fd 1 still points at the terminal when the copy is made, and is only redirected afterwards. Thinking of redirection as 'linking names' instead of copying descriptors is the trap.

exam.prompt: Assume only fds 0, 1 and 2 are open at start. What does this print?
exam.explain: `dup` returns the lowest unused descriptor, 3, now referring to the same open file description as fd 1. Writing to fd 3 would also appear on stdout. Use `dup2` when you need a specific number.

exam.prompt: Connecting to virtual memory (Module 3): a process using 2 GiB of RAM calls `fork`, and the call returns in well under a millisecond. How?
options: fork copies the 2 GiB using DMA hardware in parallel
fork copies only the page tables and marks pages read-only and shared (copy-on-write); a page is physically copied only when parent or child writes to it
The child shares the parent's memory permanently, like a thread
fork defers the whole copy until the child calls exec
exam.explain: Copy-on-write makes `fork` cost proportional to the page tables, not the data. A write to a shared page faults, and the kernel copies just that 4 KiB page. If the child calls `exec` right away, almost nothing is ever copied. Unlike threads, writes stay private after the copy.

exam.prompt: Which of these is a system call rather than an ordinary library function?
exam.explain: `write` is a thin wrapper around a trap into the kernel. `printf` formats text in user space and eventually calls `write`; `strlen` and `qsort` never leave user mode.

exam.prompt: Your HTTP server process exits silently, with no error message, whenever a client disconnects in the middle of a large download. What is the most likely cause?
options: The kernel kills processes with slow clients

Writing to a socket whose peer has closed raises SIGPIPE, whose default action terminates the process; ignore it (`signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN)` or `MSG_NOSIGNAL`) and handle the `EPIPE` error from `write`/`send` instead
The socket buffer overflowed and corrupted the stack
exam.explain: Sockets behave like pipes here: writing with no reader sends SIGPIPE, and the default action kills the process without a message. Once it is ignored, `write` returns -1 with `errno == EPIPE` and the server can close that connection and carry on.

modules.title: Concurrency
modules.summary: Run code in parallel without corrupting it: threads, races, mutexes and condition variables, deadlock avoidance, and atomics with memory ordering.

lessons.title: Threads
lessons.objective: By the end you can create and join POSIX threads, pass each one its own arguments, and say what threads share and what they do not.
concept: A **thread** is an independent stream of execution inside a process. Each thread has its own registers, program counter and **stack**; all threads of a process share the same address space: code, globals, the heap and open file descriptors. That makes threads cheap to create (tens of microseconds, versus a full `fork`) and lets them communicate through ordinary memory, which is both their power and the source of every bug in this module.

POSIX threads: `pthread_create(&tid, NULL, fn, arg)` starts `fn(arg)` in a new thread, where `fn` takes and returns a `void *`. `pthread_join(tid, &ret)` waits for it to finish and collects the return value, like `waitpid` for processes. Compile with `-pthread`. The safest design gives each thread its **own** input and output slot, for example `struct job { const int *data; size_t n; long result; }`, so threads never write to the same memory.

**Concurrency** means several tasks in progress at once; **parallelism** means actually running at the same instant on different cores. Threads give you parallelism in C. In CPython, the GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads speed up I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound work; use `multiprocessing`, or the optional free-threaded build available since Python 3.13. A classic C bug: passing `&i` from a loop to every thread, so they all read the same, changing variable.

questions.prompt: Which of these is private to each thread rather than shared by all threads in a process?
questions.explain: Each thread gets its own stack (and registers). Globals, the heap and the fd table belong to the process. Note that a thread *can* still reach another thread's stack through a pointer, which is legal but dangerous once that frame returns.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: Thread 0 sums 1..50 (1275) into `part[0]` and thread 1 sums 51..100 (3775) into `part[1]`. They never write the same element, and `pthread_join` makes their results visible to `main`, so the output is always 5050 regardless of scheduling.

questions.prompt: A CPU-bound pure-Python function takes 8 s. You run it in 4 `threading.Thread`s, each doing a quarter of the work, on a 4-core machine with standard CPython (GIL enabled). Roughly how long does it take?
questions.explain: The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, so the quarters run one after another (with some switching overhead): about 8 s. `multiprocessing` gives about 2 s because each process has its own interpreter and GIL. Threads still help for I/O-bound work, since the GIL is released while waiting.

questions.prompt: Each thread is meant to print its own id 0-3, but they often print things like `4 4 2 4`. What is wrong?
options: `pthread_create` must be called in reverse order
Every thread receives the address of the same loop variable `i`, which keeps changing (and is gone after the loop); pass each thread its own storage, such as `&ids[i]` or `(void *)(long)i`
Threads need to be joined before they start
questions.explain: All four threads dereference `&i` at some later moment, by which time `main` has advanced `i` (to 4 when the loop ends) or its scope has ended. Give each thread its own argument: an element of an array that outlives the threads, or the value itself cast into the pointer.

lessons.why: Threads let one program use many cores and stay responsive while waiting. They also introduce the hardest bugs you'll meet, so start with what is shared.

terms.d: An independent stream of execution with its own registers and stack.
Threads share the address space: globals, heap and open files.
Start a thread / wait for it and collect its result.
Tasks in progress at once vs running at the same instant on different cores.

mistakes.wrong: Passing `&i` from a loop gives each thread its own `i`.
mistakes.right: All threads see the same variable, which keeps changing. Give each thread its own argument.

mistakes.wrong: Python threads run Python code in parallel on many cores.
mistakes.right: In CPython the GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time; use processes for CPU-bound work.

Always join threads you start.
Give each thread its own argument storage.

lessons.title: Race conditions
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how `counter++` loses updates, identify data races and check-then-act races in code, and detect them with ThreadSanitizer.
concept: `counter++` looks atomic but compiles to three steps: **load** counter into a register, **add** 1, **store** it back. If two threads interleave those steps, both can load the same old value and both store old + 1: one increment vanishes. Run two threads doing a million increments each and you get some number below two million that changes from run to run. The outcome depends on timing: that is a **race condition**.

A **data race** is the specific, low-level case: two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and nothing synchronises them. In C and C++ a data race is **undefined behavior**, so the compiler may keep the variable in a register, merge or delete accesses, and the result can be stranger than 'some increments are lost'. The code between acquiring and releasing protection over shared data is a **critical section**, and it must execute as if atomic.

Races also hide at a higher level. **Check-then-act**: `if (balance >= amount) balance -= amount;` is broken even if each line were individually atomic, because two withdrawals can both pass the check before either subtracts. The same goes for 'if the file does not exist, create it' (a TOCTOU race). Race bugs may appear once in a thousand runs and vanish under a debugger, so use tools: compile with `-fsanitize=thread` (**ThreadSanitizer**) and it reports the two conflicting accesses with stack traces.

visual.title: How two threads lose an update (counter starts at 0)

example.explain: Build with `cc -O0 -pthread` and run it five times: the totals differ. With `-O2` you may even get exactly 2000000 or 1000000, because the compiler is allowed to transform racy code as if no other thread existed. Build with `-fsanitize=thread` and TSan points at the `counter++` line in both threads.

lessons.tryit: Run the example ten times at `-O0` and record the results. Build it with `-fsanitize=thread` and read the report (on Linux, or with a working TSan toolchain). Then write the bank-account check-then-act bug with two threads withdrawing 80 from a balance of 100, add `usleep(100)` between the check and the subtraction to make the race reliable, and observe a negative balance.

questions.prompt: Which situation is a data race?
options: Two threads read the same global variable at the same time
Two threads each write to their own element of an array
Two threads access the same variable without synchronisation, and at least one of them writes
One thread writes a variable and later joins another thread that reads it
questions.explain: A data race needs a shared location, concurrency, at least one write, and no synchronisation. Concurrent reads alone are safe; distinct array elements are distinct locations; and `pthread_join` is synchronisation that orders the write before the read.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run `counter++` 1000 times on a shared unprotected `int` that starts at 0 (think of `++` as load/add/store). Which final value is impossible?
questions.explain: Every increment adds at most 1, so 2000 is the maximum (no interleaving overlap). Lost updates can produce 1500, 1000 or even lower values. 2001 would require an increment out of thin air. (Strictly, in C this is a data race and therefore UB, which is why you never rely on any particular result.)

questions.prompt: Each line here uses atomic operations, so there is no data race. Can two concurrent `withdraw(80)` calls on a balance of 100 still drive it negative?
options: No: atomic operations make the function thread-safe
Yes: both threads can pass the check before either subtracts, so the check and the update must happen together under one lock (or as one compare-and-swap loop)
No: the second load will always see the first subtraction
Yes, but only on ARM processors
questions.explain: Atomicity of each step does not make the sequence atomic. Thread A loads 100 and passes; thread B loads 100 and passes; both subtract: -60. This check-then-act race exists on every architecture. Fix it by holding a mutex across check and update, or with a CAS loop that retries if the balance changed.

questions.prompt: A multithreaded test fails roughly once in 500 runs and never fails under the debugger. Which tool is designed to find the cause?
questions.explain: TSan instruments memory accesses and synchronisation and reports conflicting unsynchronised accesses even when the bad interleaving did not happen in that run. Memcheck finds memory errors, not races (Valgrind's Helgrind tool does find races), and `strace` shows syscalls. Debuggers change timing, which is why races 'disappear' under them.

lessons.why: Race conditions cause bugs that appear once in a million runs and vanish under the debugger. Recognising the patterns is the only reliable defence.

terms.d: The result depends on the timing of threads.
Concurrent access to one location, at least one a write, with no synchronisation: undefined behavior in C.
Code that must not run in two threads at once.
Testing a condition and acting on it as two separate steps.

mistakes.wrong: `counter++` is a single, safe operation.
mistakes.right: It's load, add, store. Two threads can interleave and lose updates.

mistakes.wrong: If my tests pass, there are no races.
mistakes.right: Races depend on timing. Use ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) to detect them.

takeaways: Any shared variable written by one thread needs synchronisation.
Check-then-act must be made atomic as a whole.
ThreadSanitizer finds data races your tests miss.

lessons.title: Mutexes and condition variables
lessons.objective: By the end you can protect shared state with a mutex and build a correct bounded producer-consumer queue with condition variables.
concept: A **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock) guarantees that only one thread at a time is between `pthread_mutex_lock(&m)` and `pthread_mutex_unlock(&m)`. A thread that calls `lock` on a held mutex sleeps until it is released. Think of a mutex as protecting an **invariant**, such as 'count equals the number of items in the buffer': every read or write of that data happens with the lock held. Locking also orders memory, so writes made before an unlock are visible to the next thread that locks.

Often a thread must wait for a condition, such as 'queue not empty'. Spinning on a flag wastes a core. A **condition variable** lets it sleep: `pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &m)` must be called with `m` held; it **atomically** releases `m` and sleeps, and before returning it re-acquires `m`. Another thread changes the state under the lock and calls `pthread_cond_signal` (wake one waiter) or `pthread_cond_broadcast` (wake all).

The rule that prevents most bugs: always wait in a **while loop** that re-checks the condition: `while (count == 0) pthread_cond_wait(&not_empty, &m);`. A woken thread is not guaranteed the condition still holds: another consumer may have taken the item first, and implementations may wake threads **spuriously**. A bounded buffer uses two condition variables, `not_empty` for consumers and `not_full` for producers, both protected by one mutex.

steps.detail: Sees count == 0, so the queue is empty

steps.label: cond_wait
steps.detail: Atomically unlocks m and sleeps on not_empty

steps.label: Producer locks m

steps.label: Consumer wakes
steps.detail: Re-acquires m inside cond_wait, loop re-checks count > 0

questions.prompt: What does `pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &m)` do?
options: Spins until `cv` is signalled, keeping `m` locked
Atomically unlocks `m` and puts the thread to sleep on `cv`; re-locks `m` before returning
questions.explain: Releasing the mutex and sleeping must be one atomic step: if they were separate, a producer could signal in the gap and the wakeup would be lost. Keeping `m` locked while sleeping would block the very thread that needs to change the condition.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each `count++` happens inside the critical section, so the load/add/store of one thread can never interleave with another's. 4 threads * 100000 = 400000, on every run. (Locking a million times is slow; Lesson 5's atomics or per-thread counters are faster.)

Signals are lost if no one is waiting
The mutex must be unlocked before calling `cond_wait`

lessons.title: Deadlock and how to avoid it
lessons.objective: By the end you can state the four conditions for deadlock, diagnose a deadlock from thread backtraces, and prevent it with lock ordering.
concept: A **deadlock** is a set of threads each waiting for a resource another one holds, so none can ever proceed. The textbook case: thread 1 locks A then tries to lock B; thread 2 locks B then tries to lock A. If each gets its first lock, both wait forever. The program does not crash; it just stops making progress with 0% CPU, which is how you recognise it in production.

Deadlock requires all four **Coffman conditions**: **mutual exclusion** (a resource is held by one thread at a time), **hold and wait** (threads hold one resource while requesting another), **no preemption** (locks cannot be forcibly taken away), and **circular wait** (a cycle in the waits-for graph). Break any one and deadlock is impossible. In practice the easiest to break is circular wait: impose a **global lock order** and always acquire in that order, for example by account id or by lock address.

Other tools: `pthread_mutex_trylock` with back-off (release everything and retry) breaks hold-and-wait; one coarse lock instead of many eliminates the cycle at a cost in parallelism; never call unknown code (callbacks, logging that locks) while holding a lock. A thread locking a non-recursive mutex it already holds deadlocks with itself. To diagnose, attach a debugger to the hung process (`gdb -p <pid>`, then `thread apply all bt`) and look for threads blocked in `pthread_mutex_lock`, each holding what the other wants.

left.title: Deadlock-prone
points: transfer(a, b) locks a, then b
transfer(b, a) locks b, then a
Run both at once: each holds one lock and waits for the other

right.title: Ordered (deadlock-free)
points: Always lock the account with the smaller id first
transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) both lock min(a, b) first
The second thread blocks on the first lock while holding nothing
No cycle is possible, so no deadlock

example.explain: Locks are always taken in increasing account id, whatever the transfer direction, so no cycle of waiting can form. The balance check and the update sit inside both locks, so this also fixes the check-then-act race from Lesson 2. (Transferring to the same account would need a special case.)

lessons.tryit: Write the naive `transfer` that locks `from` then `to`, and run two threads doing 1,000,000 transfers in opposite directions between the same two accounts until it hangs. Attach `lldb -p <pid>` or `gdb -p <pid>`, get all thread backtraces, and identify the cycle. Then apply the ordering fix and show it completes, with the total balance unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
questions.explain: The four are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Starvation (a thread never getting a resource because others keep winning) is a different liveness problem that can occur without any deadlock.

questions.prompt: Five dining philosophers each pick up the fork on their left, then the fork on their right. Which change prevents deadlock?
options: Make every philosopher wait 1 ms before picking up the right fork
Have one philosopher pick up the right fork first (equivalently, always take the lower-numbered fork first)
Add a sixth fork in the middle that nobody uses
questions.explain: If all five take their left fork at once, each waits on a neighbour: a cycle. Making one philosopher acquire in the opposite order imposes a global ordering, so a full cycle cannot form. Adding delays only changes the odds, it does not remove the cycle.

questions.prompt: A program hangs. `thread apply all bt` shows the only interesting thread blocked in `pthread_mutex_lock(&log_lock)` called from `log_msg`, called from `flush_buffers`, which was called from `log_msg`. What is wrong?
options: Two threads are in a lock-order cycle
The thread re-entered `log_msg` while already holding `log_lock`, so it waits on a (non-recursive) mutex that it holds itself
questions.explain: One thread, one lock: a self-deadlock. `log_msg` locks, calls `flush_buffers`, which logs and tries to lock again. Fixes: do not call code that may re-enter while holding the lock, split into `log_msg_locked` for internal use, or (less ideally) use a recursive mutex.

questions.prompt: Which change breaks the 'hold and wait' condition?
options: Always acquiring locks in increasing address order
Using `pthread_mutex_trylock` for the second lock and, if it fails, releasing the first lock and retrying later
questions.explain: With trylock-and-back-off, a thread never blocks while holding a lock: it either gets everything or gives up what it has. Lock ordering breaks circular wait instead. Back-off can livelock (both retry in lockstep), so add randomised delays.

terms.d: Threads each waiting for a resource another holds, so none can proceed.
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Always acquire locks in one global order to prevent cycles.
Release everything and retry if a lock isn't available.

mistakes.wrong: Deadlocks only happen with many locks.
mistakes.right: Two locks taken in opposite orders by two threads is enough.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a callback while holding a lock is harmless.
mistakes.right: Unknown code may take other locks and create a cycle. Release locks before calling out.

A global lock order is the standard fix.

lessons.title: Atomics and memory ordering
lessons.objective: By the end you can use C11 atomics for counters and compare-and-swap, and explain why publishing data between threads needs release/acquire ordering.
concept: C11's `<stdatomic.h>` provides types like `atomic_int` whose operations are indivisible: `atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1)` performs the load/add/store as one hardware operation (`lock xadd` on x86-64, `ldadd` or a load-linked/store-conditional loop on ARM64) and returns the old value. **Compare-and-swap**, `atomic_compare_exchange_strong(&x, &expected, desired)`, sets `x` to `desired` only if it currently equals `expected`; on failure it writes the current value into `expected`. CAS loops are the building block of lock-free code.

Atomics are not free. Contended atomics bounce the cache line between cores at about 50-100 ns per transfer. The same thing happens with **false sharing**: two threads writing *different* variables that sit in the same 64-byte line slow each other down. Per-thread counters padded to 64 bytes, combined at the end, beat one shared atomic by an order of magnitude.

**Memory ordering** is the subtle part. Compilers and CPUs reorder ordinary loads and stores when no single thread can tell. x86-64 is fairly strict (it only lets later loads pass earlier stores); ARM64 reorders much more. To **publish** data, the writer fills it in and then stores a flag with `memory_order_release`; the reader loads the flag with `memory_order_acquire`, and if it sees the flag it is guaranteed to see the data. `memory_order_relaxed` gives atomicity only, and the default, `seq_cst`, is the strongest and simplest. `volatile` provides none of these guarantees.

left.title: x86-64 (TSO, strong)
points: Stores become visible in program order
Only a later load may pass an earlier store
Release/acquire cost nothing extra in the generated code

right.title: ARM64 (weak)
points: Loads and stores to different addresses may be reordered
Needs ordered instructions such as stlr/ldar for release/acquire
Missing orderings show up as real bugs
The same racy code that worked on x86 can fail here (e.g. on Apple Silicon)

example.explain: The release store promises that everything written before it (`data = 42`) is visible to any thread whose acquire load reads `true`. With a plain `bool` flag the program has a data race, and on ARM64 the reader could see `ready` before `data`. Spinning is fine for a demo; real code would block on a condition variable.

lessons.tryit: Rewrite the racy counter from Lesson 2 three ways: with a mutex, with `atomic_fetch_add`, and with per-thread counters padded to 64 bytes (`struct { long n; char pad[56]; }`) summed at the end. Time each with 4 threads doing 10 million increments. Then remove the padding and measure the false-sharing penalty.

questions.prompt: What does `memory_order_relaxed` guarantee for an atomic operation?
options: Full sequential consistency with all other atomics
That the operation itself is atomic (no torn or lost updates), but no ordering of other memory accesses around it
That the value is written straight to RAM, bypassing caches
Nothing; it is the same as a plain variable
questions.explain: Relaxed operations are indivisible, so a relaxed `fetch_add` counter never loses increments, but they impose no ordering on surrounding reads and writes, so they cannot be used to publish data. No memory order bypasses the cache; coherence keeps caches consistent.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: CAS succeeds only if `x == expected`. Here x is 5, not 3, so nothing is stored, `ok` is false (0), and the current value 5 is written back into `expected`. A CAS loop uses that updated `expected` to retry without a separate load.

questions.prompt: On an ARM64 machine, a reader thread occasionally prints a stale `config` value even though it only reads after seeing `config_ready == true`. Both are plain (non-atomic) variables. What is the correct fix?
options: Make `config_ready` atomic; store it with `memory_order_release` after writing `config`, and load it with `memory_order_acquire` before reading `config`
Run the program on x86 instead
questions.explain: With plain variables this is a data race, and both the compiler and the ARM CPU may make the flag visible before the data. A release store paired with an acquire load creates a happens-before edge that orders the `config` write before the read. `volatile` prevents some compiler optimisations but gives no cross-thread ordering, and sleeping just hides the bug.

questions.prompt: Why is `volatile int flag;` not a correct way to signal between threads in C?
options: `volatile` variables cannot be written by more than one thread
`volatile` only stops the compiler optimising away accesses; it provides neither atomicity nor ordering with other memory, so concurrent access is still a data race
`volatile` forces a mutex lock on every access
questions.explain: `volatile` was designed for memory-mapped hardware registers and signal handlers. It does not emit memory barriers, so the CPU can still reorder surrounding accesses, and the C memory model still classifies concurrent non-atomic access as a race. Use `_Atomic`/`stdatomic.h` or a mutex.

project.title: A thread pool with a producer-consumer queue
project.brief: Build `pool.c`: a fixed set of worker threads that pull tasks (`void (*fn)(void *), void *arg`) from a bounded, mutex-and-condition-variable queue, with `pool_submit`, `pool_wait` (all submitted tasks done) and a clean `pool_shutdown`. Thread pools are how real servers and runtimes use cores, and this one exercises every lesson: threads, races, condition variables, deadlock avoidance and atomics.
milestones: Implement the bounded queue (`queue_push` blocks when full, `queue_pop` blocks when empty) and test it with 4 producers and 4 consumers checking the total of all items.
Create N worker threads that loop popping and running tasks; implement `pool_submit`.
Implement `pool_wait` with a pending-task counter and a condition variable that is broadcast when the counter reaches 0.
Implement `pool_shutdown` that sets a flag, broadcasts to wake all idle workers, and joins them; run under ThreadSanitizer (where available) with zero reports.
Use the pool to compute something real (for example, count primes below 50 million in 1000 chunks) and report speedup for 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers.
project.stretch: Add per-worker deques with work stealing, or replace the queue lock with a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer using release/acquire atomics, and benchmark it against the mutex version.

exam.prompt: Two threads each execute `x = x + 1;` once on a shared unprotected int `x` that starts at 5 (treat it as load, add, store). Which set lists every final value the load/add/store model allows?
exam.explain: If the two read-modify-writes do not overlap, the result is 7. If both load 5 before either stores, both store 6. Each thread stores a value at least one greater than 5, so 5 is impossible. (In real C this is a data race, and therefore UB; the model shows why.)

exam.prompt: A bank service deadlocks under load. Every `transfer(from, to)` locks `from->lock` then `to->lock`. Which change eliminates the deadlock while still allowing transfers between unrelated accounts to run in parallel?
options: Replace all account locks with one global lock
Lock the two accounts in a fixed global order (for example, lower account id first) regardless of transfer direction
exam.explain: Ordering breaks circular wait and keeps per-account parallelism. A global lock also prevents deadlock but serialises every transfer. Unlocking `from` before locking `to` removes the deadlock but breaks atomicity (money can be observed in flight or the balance check can go stale). Yielding only changes timing.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `atomic_fetch_add` returns the value from *before* the addition (like `c++`, not `++c`) and stores the sum. Returning the old value is what lets many threads each claim a unique ticket number from one counter.

exam.prompt: Connecting to caches (Module 3): 8 threads each increment their own element of `long counts[8]` in a tight loop, with no sharing of elements, yet it scales worse than 1 thread. Why, and what fixes it?
options: The elements are protected by a hidden lock
False sharing: all 8 longs fit in one 64-byte cache line, so every write invalidates that line in the other cores; pad each counter to its own cache line
The OS runs all 8 threads on one core
exam.explain: Cache coherence works on whole lines. 8 * 8 bytes = 64 bytes, one line, which ping-pongs between cores on every increment at roughly 100 ns per transfer. Giving each counter its own 64-byte line (`_Alignas(64)` or padding) lets each core keep its line in its own cache.

exam.prompt: During `pool_shutdown`, you set `shutting_down = true` under the queue mutex and call `pthread_cond_signal(&not_empty)` once, then join all 4 idle workers. The program hangs. Why?
options: `pthread_join` cannot be used on worker threads
`signal` wakes at most one waiting worker; the other three stay asleep in `cond_wait` forever. Use `pthread_cond_broadcast`, and make workers check `shutting_down` in their wait loop
The flag must be atomic, so the mutex is ignored
Workers must be detached before shutdown
exam.explain: Every worker sleeping on the condition variable needs a wakeup to notice the flag. `broadcast` wakes all of them; each re-acquires the mutex in turn, sees `shutting_down` with an empty queue, and exits, so the joins complete. The flag is protected by the mutex, so it does not need to be atomic.

exam.prompt: Connecting to processes (Module 4): which statement about threads versus processes created with `fork` is correct?
options: Threads in a process share the address space; a forked child gets its own (copy-on-write) copy
Both share the address space; only file descriptors differ
Forked children share globals with the parent
Threads each get a separate heap
exam.explain: Threads share code, globals, heap and fds; only stacks and registers are per thread. After `fork`, writes in the child go to private copies of pages, which is why a global changed in a child is not seen by the parent, while one changed in a thread is seen by every thread.

exam.prompt: Arrange the lines into a worker loop for the thread pool. A task with `fn == NULL` is the shutdown signal.
exam.explain: The worker blocks in `queue_pop` until there is a task, checks for the poison-pill task before calling through the pointer (calling `NULL` would crash), runs it, and loops. After the loop ends it returns so `pthread_join` can collect it. (A final `}` closes the function.)

exam.prompt: A lock-free queue publishes an element by writing the slot and then storing the new `tail` index. Which orderings are needed for consumers to see fully written slots?
options: Relaxed store of `tail`, relaxed load of `tail`
Release store of `tail` by the producer, acquire load of `tail` by the consumer
Acquire store of `tail`, release load of `tail`
No ordering is needed if `tail` is an `atomic_int`
exam.explain: Release on the store orders the slot write before the index update; acquire on the load orders the index read before the slot read. Together they form a happens-before edge. Relaxed gives atomicity of `tail` but not of the data it guards. Acquire applies to loads and release to stores, so option 3 has them backwards.

modules.summary: Follow a URL down to packets and back: layers, TCP's handshake and reliability, DNS, the C sockets API, and HTTP/1.1 written by hand.

lessons.title: Network layers: IP, TCP and UDP
lessons.objective: By the end you can name what each layer of the network stack adds, draw how an HTTP request is encapsulated, and choose between TCP and UDP for an application.
concept: Networking is built in **layers**, each using the one below as a black box. The **link** layer (Ethernet, Wi-Fi) moves **frames** between machines on the same local network using MAC addresses, typically with a 1500-byte MTU. The **network** layer, **IP**, moves **packets** between any two hosts on the internet using IP addresses (32-bit IPv4 like `192.168.1.10`, 128-bit IPv6), forwarded hop by hop by routers. IP is **best effort**: packets can be lost, duplicated or reordered, and a TTL counter stops them looping forever.

The **transport** layer adds **ports** (16-bit numbers) so many programs on one host can talk at once, and comes in two main flavours. **TCP** gives a reliable, ordered **byte stream** over an unreliable network, at the cost of a connection setup and of waiting for lost data to be resent. **UDP** sends individual **datagrams** with only ports and a checksum: no connection, no retransmission, no ordering. DNS queries, games, voice calls and QUIC (HTTP/3) build on UDP.

The **application** layer is the protocol your program speaks: HTTP, DNS, SSH. On the way out each layer wraps the data from above in its own header, which is **encapsulation**: an HTTP request becomes the payload of a TCP segment (20-byte header), inside an IPv4 packet (20-byte header), inside an Ethernet frame (14-byte header plus a 4-byte checksum). On the way in, each layer strips its header and hands the payload up. Home routers also rewrite addresses and ports with **NAT** so many devices can share one public IPv4 address.

import socket

recv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)   # UDP
recv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))            # port 0: let the OS pick a free port
addr = recv.getsockname()

send.sendto(b"ping", addr)              # no connection, just one datagram

print(data, "from port", src[1])

questions.prompt: Which layer introduces port numbers?
questions.explain: IP addresses get a packet to a host; ports, in the TCP or UDP header, pick the program on that host. That is why a socket is identified by IP address plus port. HTTP runs on top of them and only uses a port by convention (80, 443).

questions.prompt: On a link with a 1500-byte MTU, how much application data can one TCP segment carry if the IPv4 and TCP headers are 20 bytes each with no options?
questions.explain: The MTU limits the IP packet: 1500 - 20 (IP) - 20 (TCP) = 1460 bytes, the usual TCP maximum segment size. The 14-byte Ethernet header is outside the MTU, so subtracting it (1446) double-counts.

import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.0.0/16")
print(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.10") in net, ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.0.0/24").num_addresses)

questions.prompt: You are designing a voice-chat app. Why do such apps typically send audio over UDP instead of TCP?

A lost audio packet is useless by the time it could be resent, and TCP's in-order delivery would stall all later audio waiting for it (head-of-line blocking); with UDP the app skips the gap
questions.explain: TCP's reliability is a liability for real-time media: one loss delays everything behind it by at least a round trip. With UDP, the app decides: conceal the missing 20 ms and keep playing. UDP gives no delivery or timing guarantee and no encryption; apps add those themselves (as WebRTC and QUIC do).

lessons.title: TCP: handshake and reliability
lessons.objective: By the end you can trace the three-way handshake with sequence and acknowledgement numbers, explain how TCP recovers from loss, and estimate connection latency in round trips.
concept: Before any data flows, TCP performs a **three-way handshake**. The client sends **SYN** with an initial sequence number x. The server replies **SYN-ACK** with its own sequence number y and acknowledgement x + 1. The client answers **ACK** with acknowledgement y + 1. Both sides now know each other's starting numbers and that packets flow both ways. It costs one round trip (**RTT**) before the client can send its request, which is why connection reuse matters so much.

TCP numbers **bytes**, not packets. Each segment carries the sequence number of its first byte, and the receiver replies with a **cumulative ACK**: the number of the next byte it expects. If a segment is lost, the sender notices either by a **retransmission timeout** (RTO, estimated from measured RTTs) or by **three duplicate ACKs** (fast retransmit), and resends. The receiver puts out-of-order data back in order before handing it to the application, so your `recv` always sees a correct byte stream.

Two controls govern speed. **Flow control**: the receiver advertises a window, the number of bytes it can buffer, and the sender never exceeds it. **Congestion control**: the sender keeps a congestion window that starts small, roughly doubles every RTT during **slow start**, and is cut when loss signals congestion (algorithms such as Reno, CUBIC and BBR). Closing uses **FIN** and **ACK** in each direction, after which the side that closed first waits in **TIME_WAIT** so stray old packets cannot confuse a new connection.

Then compute how long a 10 MB download takes on a 50 ms RTT link if the congestion window starts at 10 segments of 1460 bytes and doubles each RTT, ignoring the bandwidth limit.

questions.prompt: What is the order of the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.explain: The client's SYN proposes a sequence number; the server's SYN-ACK acknowledges it and proposes its own; the client's ACK acknowledges the server's. Each side must hear an acknowledgement of its own SYN, which takes three messages, not two.

questions.prompt: A client sends SYN with seq = 1000, and the server replies SYN-ACK with seq = 7000. What acknowledgement numbers do the SYN-ACK and the client's final ACK carry?
questions.explain: An ACK names the next byte expected. A SYN consumes one sequence number, so after the client's SYN at 1000 the server expects 1001, and after the server's SYN at 7000 the client expects 7001.

questions.prompt: A receiver has received bytes 1-1000 and 2001-3000 of a stream; bytes 1001-2000 were lost. What acknowledgement number does it send?
questions.explain: TCP ACKs are cumulative: they name the next byte needed to continue the stream in order, 1001, however much later data is buffered. Repeated ACKs of 1001 as more data arrives are the duplicate ACKs that trigger fast retransmit. (SACK options can additionally report the 2001-3000 block.)

questions.prompt: The RTT to a server is 100 ms. Ignoring DNS and transfer time, about how long after starting does the first byte of an HTTPS response arrive on a brand-new connection using TCP and TLS 1.3?
questions.explain: TCP handshake: 1 RTT. TLS 1.3 handshake: 1 RTT. Request and first byte of the response: 1 RTT. Total 300 ms. TLS 1.2 needs one more round trip (400 ms), and HTTP/3 over QUIC merges the transport and TLS handshakes (200 ms). Reusing a kept-alive connection costs only the last 100 ms.

lessons.why: TCP behaviour explains slow page loads, stalled downloads and why connection reuse matters. Counting round trips is how you estimate network latency.

terms.d: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: one round trip before data flows.
Numbers bytes, not packets, so the receiver can order and acknowledge them.
The number of the next byte the receiver expects.
The sender's window grows with slow start and shrinks on loss.

mistakes.wrong: TCP numbers each packet 1, 2, 3.
mistakes.right: It numbers bytes. Each segment carries the sequence number of its first byte.

mistakes.wrong: A new connection can send at full speed immediately.
mistakes.right: Slow start begins small and doubles each round trip, so short transfers on new connections are slow.

takeaways: Handshake costs one RTT; TLS adds more.
Loss is recovered by timeout or three duplicate ACKs.
Reusing connections avoids handshakes and slow start.

lessons.title: DNS: turning names into addresses
lessons.objective: By the end you can trace a DNS lookup from your laptop to an authoritative server, read the common record types, and debug a resolution failure with `dig`.
concept: Your program wants `api.example.com` but IP needs an address. **DNS** is a distributed, hierarchical, cached database for that mapping. Names are read right to left: the **root** (`.`), then a **top-level domain** (`com`), then `example.com`, whose owner runs **authoritative** name servers that hold the real records. No single server knows everything; each level delegates the next with **NS** records.

Your OS has a **stub resolver** (behind `getaddrinfo`) that first checks `/etc/hosts` and local caches, then asks a **recursive resolver**: your router, your ISP's, or a public one like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. The recursive resolver does the work: it asks a root server, which refers it to the `.com` servers, which refer it to example.com's servers, which answer. Every answer carries a **TTL** in seconds, and every resolver along the way caches it for that long, so most lookups never leave the first cache.

Common record types: **A** (name to IPv4), **AAAA** (name to IPv6), **CNAME** (alias to another name), **MX** (mail servers), **NS** (delegation), **TXT** (arbitrary text, used for domain verification). Queries normally travel over **UDP port 53** in one packet each way, falling back to TCP for large answers; DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS encrypt them. Debug with `dig example.com A`, `dig +short`, `dig @8.8.8.8 example.com` to bypass your resolver, and `dig +trace` to watch the delegation chain.

steps.detail: getaddrinfo(): /etc/hosts and OS cache miss, ask the recursive resolver

steps.label: Root server
steps.detail: 'I don't know, ask the .com servers' (NS referral)

steps.label: .com TLD server
steps.detail: 'Ask example.com's name servers' (NS referral)

steps.label: Authoritative server
steps.detail: 'www.example.com A <address>, TTL 3600'

example.code:
dig +short example.com A            # just the IPv4 address(es)
dig example.com AAAA                # full answer: look at the TTL column
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com            # ask a specific resolver directly
dig +trace www.example.com          # follow root -> com -> example.com yourself
dig example.com MX +short           # mail servers, with priorities
example.explain: Run the plain `dig` twice in a row against the same resolver: the TTL in the second answer is lower, because the resolver is counting down its cached copy. `+trace` makes `dig` act as its own recursive resolver, so you see each referral.

lessons.tryit: Run `dig +trace` for a domain you use daily and write down each server that answered and what it said. Then pick a site behind a CDN and use `dig` to find its CNAME chain. questions.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: AAAA ("quad A", four times the size of an A record's 32 bits) holds a 128-bit IPv6 address. A holds IPv4, CNAME points to another name, and MX names mail servers.

questions.prompt: You change your site's A record. Its TTL was 3600. With resolvers that honour TTLs, how long can some clients keep getting the old address?
options: Up to about one hour after the change, until cached copies expire
Zero: DNS changes are pushed to all resolvers immediately
Exactly 24 hours, the global propagation time
questions.explain: DNS has no push. Each resolver that cached the old record keeps serving it until its TTL runs out, up to 3600 seconds. That is why you lower the TTL a day before a planned migration. 'Propagation takes 24-48 hours' is folklore about long TTLs.

questions.prompt: DNS messages encode names as length-prefixed labels. What does this Python print?
questions.code:
name = "www.example.com"
wire = b"".join(bytes([len(p)]) + p.encode() for p in name.split(".")) + b"\x00"
print(wire)
questions.explain: Each label is preceded by a length byte (3, 7, 3), and a zero-length label (the root) ends the name. Python prints bytes below 0x20 as `\x..` escapes. Building this by hand is the first step of writing your own DNS client over a UDP socket.

questions.prompt: `curl https://api.internal.example` fails with `Could not resolve host`, but `curl -k https://10.0.4.7` (its known address) works. What is the most useful next step?
options: Run `dig api.internal.example` and `dig @<your-resolver> api.internal.example` to see which resolver is answering and whether the record exists
questions.explain: Reaching the address directly proves the network path and server are fine, so the failure is in name resolution: a missing record, a wrong resolver (for example, a VPN's internal DNS not in use), or a stale negative cache. `dig` shows exactly which server answered and with what status (NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL).

Holds the actual records for a domain.
How long a record may be cached.
A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (delegation), TXT.

mistakes.right: Resolvers keep cached answers until the TTL expires.

mistakes.wrong: My computer asks the root servers directly.
mistakes.right: Your stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which does the walk and caches it.

lessons.title: The sockets API in C
lessons.objective: By the end you can write a TCP server and client in C with `socket`, `bind`, `listen`, `accept`, `connect`, `send` and `recv`, handling byte order and partial reads.
concept: A **socket** is a file descriptor for a network endpoint. A TCP server calls `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)`, sets `SO_REUSEADDR` so it can restart without waiting out TIME_WAIT, `bind`s it to an address and port, and calls `listen(fd, backlog)` to start accepting connections. Each `accept(fd, ...)` blocks until a client connects and returns a **new** descriptor for that one connection; the listening socket stays open for the next client.

A client resolves the name with `getaddrinfo` (which handles DNS and IPv4/IPv6), creates a socket, and calls `connect`, which performs the TCP handshake. Both sides then use `send`/`recv` (or `write`/`read`) and finally `close`. Multi-byte numbers in protocol headers, such as the port in `struct sockaddr_in`, are in **network byte order** (big-endian), so convert with `htons`/`htonl` and back with `ntohs`/`ntohl`. Forgetting `htons(8080)` binds you to port 36895 on a little-endian machine.

TCP is a **byte stream**, not a message queue. `recv` returns whatever has arrived, from 1 byte up to your buffer size; two `send`s can arrive in one `recv`, and one `send` can arrive in pieces. `recv` returning **0** means the peer closed the connection (EOF), and `send` may write fewer bytes than asked. So you always loop, and you need **framing**: a delimiter (HTTP headers end with a blank line) or a length prefix. A server that calls `accept` and handles one client at a time stalls everyone behind a slow client; real servers use `fork`, threads or `poll`/`epoll`/`kqueue`.

steps.detail: Create an endpoint: an fd with no address yet

steps.label: bind()
steps.detail: Attach it to 0.0.0.0:8080 (port via htons)

steps.label: listen()
steps.detail: Mark it passive; the kernel queues handshakes (backlog)

steps.label: accept()
steps.detail: Block until a client connects; returns a NEW fd per connection

steps.label: recv()/send()
steps.detail: Loop: partial reads and writes are normal; 0 = peer closed

steps.detail: Close the connection fd; keep the listening fd for the next client

example.explain: Run it and connect with `nc 127.0.0.1 8080`: everything you type comes back. The inner loop runs until `recv` returns 0 (the client closed) or -1 (an error). Open a second `nc` while the first is connected and notice that it gets no echo until the first one quits: one client at a time.

lessons.tryit: Build the echo server, then write a C client that uses `getaddrinfo` and `connect`, sends a 1 MB buffer, and reads the echo back, counting how many `recv` calls it took and the size of each. Then add a 4-byte big-endian length prefix to each message on both sides, so the receiver knows exactly where each message ends.

questions.prompt: What does `accept()` return on a listening TCP socket?
options: A new file descriptor for the one accepted connection, while the listening socket keeps listening
The same descriptor, now connected to the client
questions.explain: Each accepted connection gets its own fd, which is how one server talks to many clients. The client's address is optionally written into the `struct sockaddr` you pass to `accept`; the return value is the descriptor (or -1).

questions.prompt: Network byte order is big-endian. What does this print?
questions.explain: 8080 = 0x1F90. Big-endian sends the most significant byte first: 0x1F = 31, then 0x90 = 144. This is what `htons` arranges in memory; writing it out with shifts like this is endian-independent, which is why it is a good way to build headers.

questions.prompt: A client calls `send` twice, each with a 100-byte message. The server does one `recv(fd, buf, 4096, 0)`. What can it return?
options: Anything from 1 to 200 bytes: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries, so the server must loop and frame messages itself
Exactly 200 bytes, because the buffer is big enough
An error, because 4096 is larger than the message
questions.explain: TCP delivers bytes in order but has no idea where your messages begin and end. The two sends may be coalesced into one segment, or the first may arrive split. Correct code reads in a loop until it has a full message by its framing rule (length prefix, delimiter, or HTTP's Content-Length).

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines of a minimal TCP server that sends one greeting to the first client.
questions.explain: Each call depends on the previous one: a socket must exist before it can be bound, bound before it listens, listening before it can accept, and you can only send on and close the connection descriptor that `accept` returned.
