lessons.why: Every networked program, from web servers to databases, is built on sockets. Handling byte order and partial reads correctly is what makes them reliable.

terms.d: A file descriptor for a network endpoint.
Returns a new socket for each client; the listening socket stays open.
Big-endian; convert with `htons`/`ntohs`.
Marking where messages begin and end in a byte stream, by length prefix or delimiter.

mistakes.wrong: One `send` arrives as exactly one `recv`.
mistakes.right: TCP is a byte stream: data can arrive split or merged. Loop until you have a full message.

mistakes.wrong: `recv` returning 0 means no data yet.
mistakes.right: It means the peer closed the connection.

takeaways: Server: socket, bind, listen, accept. Client: getaddrinfo, socket, connect.
Always loop on `send` and `recv`.
Design a framing scheme for your messages.

lessons.title: HTTP from scratch: what happens when you type a URL
lessons.objective: By the end you can narrate every step from typing a URL to seeing a page, and write and parse a raw HTTP/1.1 request and response by hand.
concept: Type `https://example.com/docs/index.html` and press Enter. The browser **parses the URL**: scheme `https` (so port 443 by default; `http` means 80), host `example.com`, path `/docs/index.html`. It **resolves** the host with DNS (Lesson 3), opens a **TCP connection** to that address and port (Lesson 2), and, for HTTPS, runs a **TLS handshake**: it sends the hostname (SNI), checks the server's certificate chain against trusted roots, and agrees on encryption keys. Only then is a single byte of HTTP sent.

HTTP/1.1 is plain text with lines ending in `\r\n`. A request is a request line (`GET /docs/index.html HTTP/1.1`), headers (`Host: example.com` is mandatory, because one IP address can serve many sites), and a blank line. A response is a status line (`HTTP/1.1 200 OK`), headers such as `Content-Type: text/html` and `Content-Length: 1256`, a blank line, then the body. The client knows where the body ends from `Content-Length`, from `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, or because the server closes the connection.

Status codes group by first digit: 2xx success (`200`), 3xx redirect or cache (`301`, `304 Not Modified`), 4xx client error (`404`, `403`), 5xx server error (`500`, `503`). HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default so the next request skips the handshakes. The browser then parses the HTML, discovers CSS, JS and images, fetches them (often over the same connection, or multiplexed with HTTP/2 or QUIC-based HTTP/3), builds the DOM, lays it out, and paints pixels.

steps.label: Parse URL
steps.detail: scheme https -> port 443, host example.com, path /

steps.label: DNS
steps.detail: Cache or recursive resolver -> A/AAAA record (Lesson 3)

steps.label: TCP handshake
steps.detail: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK to port 443: 1 RTT (Lesson 2)

steps.label: TLS handshake
steps.detail: SNI, certificate check, key exchange: 1 RTT with TLS 1.3

steps.label: HTTP request/response
steps.detail: GET / HTTP/1.1 + Host header -> 200 OK + headers + body

steps.label: Render

example.code:
import socket

host = "example.com"
req = (f"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host}\r\n"
       "Connection: close\r\n\r\n")
with socket.create_connection((host, 80)) as s:    # DNS + TCP handshake
    s.sendall(req.encode())
    resp = b""
    while chunk := s.recv(4096):                    # loop until the server closes
        resp += chunk
head, _, body = resp.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
print(head.decode().splitlines()[0])               # e.g. HTTP/1.1 200 OK
print(len(body), "body bytes")
example.explain: This is a complete HTTP client with no HTTP library: `create_connection` does the DNS lookup and TCP handshake, the request is three header lines and a blank line, and `Connection: close` lets you read until EOF instead of parsing `Content-Length`. It uses port 80 because plain sockets do not do TLS; wrap the socket with the `ssl` module for HTTPS.

lessons.tryit:
Run the example, then send the same request by hand with `printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

' | nc example.com 80`. Remove the Host header and see what changes. Then write out, in your own words and from memory, every step from Enter to pixels for `https://news.ycombinator.com/`, naming the protocol and port at each network step.

questions.prompt: Which request header is mandatory in HTTP/1.1?
questions.explain: One IP address often hosts many sites, so the server needs `Host` to know which one you want; HTTP/1.1 servers must reject requests without it with 400. `User-Agent` and `Accept` are optional, and `Content-Length` is needed only when a request has a body.

questions.prompt: What does this Python print?
questions.code:
raw = b"HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Length: 9
Content-Type: text/plain

not found"
head, body = raw.split(b"

", 1)
status = head.split(b"
")[0].split(b" ")[1]
print(int(status), len(body))

questions.prompt: For the URL `http://example.com:8080/a/b?q=1#top`, which TCP port does the browser connect to, and what is the request line?
questions.explain: An explicit `:8080` overrides the default port 80. The request target is the path plus query; the fragment (`#top`) is never sent to the server, because it only tells the browser where to scroll. The host goes in the `Host: example.com:8080` header.

questions.prompt: Your static file server sends `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, a `Content-Type` header, a blank line and the file, but no `Content-Length`, and it keeps the connection open. The browser shows a spinner forever. Why?
options: Without `Content-Length` (or chunked encoding) the only way to know the body has ended is connection close, which never comes, so the browser keeps waiting for more body
Files must be sent before the headers
questions.explain: Framing again: HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default, so the body's end must be marked. Send `Content-Length: <file size>`, use chunked encoding, or send `Connection: close` and close the socket after the body.

project.title: An HTTP/1.1 static file server from raw sockets
project.brief: Write `httpd.c`, which serves files from a directory over HTTP/1.1 using only the sockets API: parse request lines and headers, send correct status codes, `Content-Length` and `Content-Type`, and support keep-alive. It joins every module of this stage: C strings and buffers, file descriptors, processes or threads for concurrency, and TCP framing.
milestones: Accept connections on a configurable port and answer every request with a fixed `200 OK` and a correct `Content-Length`; test with `curl -v`.

Parse the request line and headers robustly (read until `\r\n\r\n`, handle partial `recv`s, reject over-long requests with `431`), and serve files from a document root with `Content-Type` based on the extension.
Return `404` for missing files, `405` for methods other than GET/HEAD, and `403` for any path that escapes the document root (for example, `/../etc/passwd`).
Support persistent connections: handle several requests per connection, and honour `Connection: close`.
Handle many clients concurrently using your Module 5 thread pool (or `fork` per connection), and ignore SIGPIPE so disconnecting clients cannot kill the server.
Load-test with `ab -n 10000 -c 50` or `wrk`, and report requests per second and any errors.
project.stretch: Replace the thread pool with a single-threaded event loop on `poll` (or `epoll`/`kqueue`) and non-blocking sockets, and compare throughput and memory use with 1000 concurrent idle connections.

exam.prompt: Arrange the steps a browser takes for `https://example.com/` on a cold start.
lines: Parse the URL into scheme, host, port and path
Resolve example.com to an IP address with DNS
Open a TCP connection to port 443 (three-way handshake)
Run the TLS handshake and verify the certificate
Send `GET / HTTP/1.1` with a Host header
Receive the response, parse the HTML and render it
exam.explain: Each step needs the previous one: you cannot look up a host you have not parsed, connect without an address, negotiate TLS without a connection, send encrypted HTTP before keys exist, or render before the bytes arrive.

exam.prompt: A server's SYN-ACK has seq = 3000 and ack = 801. What sequence number did the client's SYN carry?
exam.explain: The ack is the next byte the server expects, and a SYN consumes one sequence number, so the client's SYN had seq 800. The client's following ACK will carry ack = 3001.

exam.prompt: Connecting to pipes (Module 4): in your HTTP server, `recv` on a connection returns 0. What does it mean and what should the server do?
options: No data yet; call `recv` again immediately
The peer has closed its side (EOF), just like `read` returning 0 on a pipe whose writers have all closed; finish up and `close` the connection fd
The request was empty; send `400 Bad Request` and keep reading
exam.explain: On stream sockets, as on pipes, 0 means end of stream. 'No data yet' blocks (or returns -1 with `EAGAIN` on a non-blocking socket), and errors return -1. Looping on 0 would spin forever at 100% CPU.

exam.prompt: What does this Python print?
exam.code:
req = "GET /docs/a.html?x=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

"
method, target, version = req.split("
")[0].split(" ")
print(target.split("?")[0])
exam.explain: The request line has three space-separated parts: method, target and version. The target includes the query string, so splitting on `?` leaves the path a file server maps to disk. Real servers must also percent-decode it and check it for `..`.

exam.prompt: Your file server maps the request path straight onto the document root: `snprintf(full, sizeof full, "%s%s", root, path)`. What does `GET /../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1` do, and what is the fix?
options: Returns 404, since the file is outside the root
Can serve `/etc/passwd` (path traversal); resolve the full path with `realpath` and refuse with 403 unless it still starts with the document root
Crashes the server with a buffer overflow
Nothing; the kernel blocks `..` in paths
exam.explain: `..` is handled by the kernel when opening the file, so the string concatenation walks out of the root. Canonicalise (after percent-decoding, since `%2e%2e` is also `..`) and check the prefix, or open files relative to a directory fd with `openat` and reject any `..` segment.

exam.prompt: Which transport and port do ordinary DNS queries use by default?
exam.explain: Plain DNS uses UDP port 53: one small request, one reply, no handshake. It falls back to TCP port 53 for large responses. TCP 443 is HTTPS (and DNS-over-HTTPS), and UDP 123 is NTP.

exam.prompt: Connecting to concurrency (Module 5): your server handles one connection at a time in its `accept` loop, and with keep-alive a single idle browser tab freezes the site for everyone. What is the best structural fix?
options: Hand each accepted connection to a worker (thread pool, or `fork`), or multiplex connections with `poll`/`epoll`, and add an idle timeout
exam.explain: A blocking `recv` on one idle connection stops the loop from reaching `accept` again. Concurrency (threads or processes) or an event loop lets one slow client wait without blocking the others, and idle timeouts stop abandoned connections from holding resources forever. The backlog only sizes the queue of not-yet-accepted connections.

exam.prompt: Connecting to Module 2: a C program writes the 16-bit port 8080 (0x1F90) into a packet header with `memcpy(hdr, &port, 2)` on a little-endian machine, without `htons`. Which bytes go on the wire, and which port does the receiver read?
exam.explain: Little-endian memory holds the low byte first, so `memcpy` copies 0x90 then 0x1F. The receiver reads them as big-endian, giving 0x901F = 36895. `htons` swaps the bytes on little-endian hosts (and does nothing on big-endian ones) so the wire format is always correct.
